And there arose a great storm of wind, and the waves beat into the ship, so that it was now full. And he was in the hinder part of the ship, asleep on a pillow: and they awake him, and say unto him, Master, carest thou not that we perish? And he arose, and rebuked the wind, and said unto the sea, Peace, be still. And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm. And he said unto them, Why are ye so fearful? how is it that ye have no faith? And they feared exceedingly, and said one to another, What manner of man is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him? Mark 4:37-41

Many times, I have read this passage and wondered what we are to derive from it. It seems to be a story that generates more questions than it solves. We often like to think of Jesus as the relational form of the Godhead; a sort of go-between, between us and the Almighty God. But here, in our scriptural passage, His behavior is almost unthinkable in human terms. How could Christ sleep in such a storm, much less in a boat filling with water? We can believe that He is Master of the wind and seas, and they must bow at His command, but does He expect us to do the same? Would our compassionate Christ expect us to be calm and fearless in such dire straits? Is all exhibition of fear the fruit of our lack of faith? These probing questions are disturbing, for we all would hope that our faith in Him is strong enough to secure our salvation, yet experience has taught us that our own walk through the troublesome pastures of life has produced nothing more noble than the harrowing bleating of the disciples.

Why are ye so fearful? How is it that ye have no faith? The questions seem almost out of place coming from our Saviour, almost as though He is not as patient and longsuffering as we had hoped. But Christ has placed a definitive expectation upon His disciples that is not beyond their attainment. Was He calling on them to rebuke the storm themselves? Should they have awakened Him sooner? Did he expect them to quietly row on in confident assurance? The Scripture here supplies us with few answers, but we do know that there is an abiding lesson here concerning fear and faith.

Storms are a common part of life, and no major dilemma is pleasant. While Paul sailed toward Rome, they experienced a time …when neither sun nor stars in many days appeared, and no small tempest lay on us, all hope that we should be saved was then taken away –Acts 27:20. In the midst of a cloudy and hopeless situation there is one bell that continues to toll clear and bright: There is a peace that can be apprehended even in the most dreadful circumstances. Paul had spent a precarious …night and a day I have been in the deep –2 Corinthians 11:25, yet he did not demand the wind and sea to submit to his authority. Rather, he states that in the midst of the storm …there stood by me this night the angel of God, whose I am, and whom I serve, Saying, Fear not, Paul… –Acts 27:23-24. This is a scene similar to the peril being endured by the disciples (in our text for today) yet we see a different outcome. Paul was comforted and commended while the disciples received rebuke.

While bobbing about in the clutches of a potential watery grave, the disciples cried out: …Master, carest thou not that we perish? –Mark 4:38. How natural it is for us all to thrust our frustration and blame upon another. To think that some apathetic person is shirking their responsibility is very disheartening. In like fashion …the shipmaster came to him [Jonah], and said unto him, What meanest thou, O sleeper? arise, call upon thy God, if so be that God will think upon us, that we perish not –Jonah 1:6.

There seems to be an edge to the shipmaster’s rebuke very similar to the disciple’s response to the sleeping Jesus. Christ finds no pleasure in allowing trouble to visit us, but there seems to be no other veritable vehicle of grace wherewith His peace can flood our souls. If there first be no valley, how shall we value the mountaintop? If there be no thorns, how shall we enjoy the rose? If there first be no storm, how shall we appreciate the calm? Paul suffered the same despair being …pressed out of measure, above strength, insomuch that we despaired even of life –2 Corinthians 1:8. Yet he carried within his breast a visionary anchor for his soul.

For he commandeth, and raiseth the stormy wind, which lifteth up the waves thereof. They mount up to the heaven, they go down again to the depths: their soul is melted because of trouble. They reel to and fro, and stagger like a drunken man, and are at their wits’ end. Then they cry unto the LORD in their trouble, and he bringeth them out of their distresses. He maketh the storm a calm, so that the waves thereof are still. Then are they glad because they be quiet; so he bringeth them unto their desired haven –Psalm 107:25-30.

The Desired Haven…

Somehow, we have embraced the thought that the desired haven of rest is an earthly euphoric utopia void of any storms. The shipmaster in charge of guiding the vessel en route to Rome thought that …the haven was not commodious to winter in … supposing that they had obtained their purpose… –Acts 27:12-13, so he set sail at the first hint of approval from the soft south wind. But the haven Christ promotes is a harbor that is free from fretful fear and fledgling faith. This is a peace … not as the world giveth, give I unto you. Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid –John 14:27. This rest is ours to be had just by sailing with Christ and trusting Him to guide us through each storm.

The tenacious storms of adversity can arise without warning as quickly as …a tempestuous wind, called Euroclydon –Acts 27:14. These tempestuous winds carry an amazing audacity to jolt any relationship. To feel tense and alert in the midst of stressful situations is but human nature. Our central medulla gland unleashes a powerful hormone called adrenaline into our system, our muscles become tense, our mind focuses, so that we are aroused and prepared for fight or flight. This is not necessarily anxiety but a natural response. As humans, we have a divine capacity to reason in the midst of extreme passion and pressure. The disciples did not know what Jesus would do. They only knew that this situation was out of control. Here is where they made their major mistake. Christ knew Who was in control. Paul knew Who was in control. Even Jonah knew why the tempest had arisen. Our faith is bound to fail when anxiety escalates, and we think we must control the raging trials about us. We may have a noble agenda and a sincere heart and still find our faltering faith frazzled. We mistakenly marvel that God sits in heaven and does nothing. We faithfully launch our prayers upward, but the heavens seem brazenly silent. We would expect that from worshippers of Baal, Buddha, and from backsliders. But it is not supposed to happen to people with strong convictions—people who are born again, attend church regularly, read their Bible, and pray on a daily basis. We must reconsider that God is not so concerned about our environmental peace, but rather that our inner soul arrives safe and sound at His haven of rest.

When we are happy, we jubilantly claim that rest, even though we have no sense of truly needing Him. His insertions into our lives often seem like interruptions. But when times get desperate and we have exhausted all our resources, we lean hard upon Him. In that excruciating hour, He often tests our sincerity and offers us nothing … nothing but silence. Christ, sleeping in our boat. Sleeping… right when we need him the most. And then the question, Why are ye so fearful? How is it that ye have no faith? Frankly, this seems hard to me—even harsh—and entirely out of character with what I would normally expect from Jesus. But the question must be answered, for it is necessary if we wish to enter His haven of rest. The winds obey Him, but they don’t obey us … or do they? We obviously cannot control the weather, our environment, our situations, or the people around us. Yet these externals are not the root cause of our anxiety. It is our own faulty premonitions that pound our soul and prevent us from entering the portal of peace. The winds that whip our vessel into a fearful frenzy are not driven from without but unleashed from within. This anxiety rides on the waves of unbelief, while Christ continues in His divine slumber, waiting until we recognize the source of our anxiety and call out in faith. These four strong winds are roused at the slightest provocation when we are…

…Preserving our Person

If we are healthy, and if things are going well in our family and finances, we may be prone to misinterpret our circumstances. It is a mistake to believe that easy sailing is a mark of God’s favor, and that trouble is a sign of His displeasure. All good and perfect gifts come from God, but a debilitating storm can fall under that category as well. Our personal surroundings are temporal while our soul is eternal. God will frequently expend our personal comforts in order to expand our faith. But great fear arises when our person is demoted. Many of our phobias arise in the absence of actual danger.

  1. The acrophobic person has a fear of heights and is afraid he will fall from the heights of any platform though it is secure and guarded well. Even if countless others have successfully stood there, he is miserably trapped in this fear, not because he is in danger, but because he has grossly overestimated his likelihood of falling and refuses to believe the truth.
  2. The zoophobic lives in fear of animals, creating images in his mind of being clawed to death or disemboweled.
  3. The claustrophobic is afraid of small, tight places, while the agoraphobic fears open places.
  4. Arachibutyrophobia is the fear of getting peanut butter stuck to the roof of your mouth.

In the face of his fear, the phobic may experience a racing heart, heavy breathing, dry mouth, perspiration, dizziness, or light-headedness. Thus, their phobias become real to them. While most will excuse their personal glitch, the truth remains that this anxiety is unfounded. When we excuse and cater to the preservation of our person, fear is inevitable. The disciples feared that they were perishing, and Christ asked them why. Is it not better …to depart, and to be with Christ; which is far better –Philippians 1:23. If we can trust Christ with our life, can we not trust him with our death?

For whosoever will save his life shall lose it; but whosoever shall lose his life for my sake and the gospel’s, the same shall save it –Mark 8:35.

…Protecting our Property

Outwardly, the life of Christ was one of the most troubled lives that was ever lived. Foxes had their dens and the birds had their nests while He lay His pillow in the back of a rocking boat groaning under tempest and tumult of the incessant waves breaking over it. But His inner haven was a sea of glass. This was partially due to the fact that He had no property to protect. Even the boat was borrowed. “Much coin, much care” states the ancient proverb, and anxiety rises when wealth falls. And one of the company said unto him, Master, speak to my brother, that he divide the inheritance with me –Luke 12:13. Jesus refused to side with him. Instead, He spoke to the covetous heart that was causing the anxiety. If Christ gives us wealth, we do not need to feel guilty. If He takes it, we do not need to feel anxiety. In the midst of the storm, we are exhorted …to be of good cheer: for there shall be no loss of any man’s life among you, but of the ship –Acts 27:22. This was ministered as healing balm to the bedraggled sailors, but to those who feel inclined to protect their property it is a sordid saga. When the rich young ruler was offered salvation in exchange for his earthly collection of trinkets, …he went away sorrowful: for he had great possessions –Matthew 19:22. Those of us who become anxious at the loss of our wealth are no less foolish.

…Perfecting our Plan

We set out on a course. Maybe we change jobs, enter into a relationship, or embark upon some new avenue of ministry. We have launched out in faith and before we know it, we are struggling. The winds and waves of ordinary life seem to be working against us. We have expectations that are not being met and it seems that Christ is not doing His part. It is not Christ, but rather it is our expectation that is the cause of our anxiety. We expect much from our investments and it is discouraging to see our efforts go for naught. Martha’s pulse quickened at the lack of help she was receiving in the kitchen. Her frustration rose while her well-planned meal remained unfinished. Her complaint is no less accusing than the disciples’ while rowing in the sea. …Lord, dost thou not care that my sister hath left me to serve alone? bid her therefore that she help me –Luke 10:40. Her anxiety was not caused by Mary’s neglect nor Christ’s indifference. Her sister was docked at the haven of rest while Martha battled the tumultuous emotions within her heart. So does the perfectionist create his own storm when his unfulfilled vision falls short of his expectations. But Christ is more concerned about faith-filled bosoms than water-filled boats.

…Pleasing all People

The Scriptures have taught us well to love our neighbor as ourselves, but that does not insinuate that we must strive and aim for their approval. It feels wonderful to be liked. It is painful to be rejected. Thus, many souls spend their waking hours seeking the approval of others. They must dress like, act like, talk like, and live like their peers. These live a life laden with stressful waves of anxiety. A flurry of “what ifs” arrive with each new acquaintance. There is no ship more fragile than a relationship. No matter how great a sacrifice we make to be loved, we will eventually encounter a disappointing squall sucking us down to the depths of despair. When our best efforts fail us and our best friends derail us, we must bring our battered vessel to the haven of rest. Inconvenient, unfortunate, unpleasant, and annoying relationships will always exist. We shall do much better to make excuses for others’ poor behavior than for our own. When we can rebuke the winds that arise within our own minds, we will immediately find ourselves at the desired haven.

There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God. For he that is entered into his rest, he also hath ceased from his own works, as God did from his. Let us labour therefore to enter into that rest… –Hebrews 4:9-11.

E sorse una grande tempesta di vento, e le onde si riversavano nella barca, tanto che essa si riempì; ed egli era nella poppa, addormentato sopra un cuscino; e lo svegliarono e gli dissero: Maestro, non ti importa che noi periamo? Ed egli si alzò, rimproverò il vento e disse al mare: Tacete, calmatevi. E il vento cessò, e ci fu una grande calma. E disse loro: Perché avete paura? Come mai non avete fede? E furono presi da grande timore e si dicevano l’un l’altro: Chi dunque è costui, che anche il vento e il mare gli obbediscono? Mark 4:37-41

Molte volte ho letto questo passo e mi sono chiesto cosa dovremmo ricavarne. Sembra una storia che genera più domande di quante ne risolva. Spesso ci piace pensare a Gesù come alla forma relazionale della Deità; una sorta di mediatore tra noi e l'Iddio Onnipotente. Ma qui, nel nostro passo scritturale, il suo comportamento è quasi impensabile in termini umani. Come poteva Cristo dormire in una tale tempesta, e tanto meno in una barca che si riempiva d'acqua? Possiamo credere che egli sia il Signore del vento e dei mari, e che essi debbano chinarsi al suo comando, ma si aspetta che noi facciamo lo stesso? Il nostro Cristo compassionevole si aspetterebbe che siamo calmi e impavidi in simili pericoli? Ogni manifestazione di paura è frutto della nostra mancanza di fede? Queste domande penetranti sono sconcertanti, perché tutti spereremmo che la nostra fede in lui sia abbastanza forte da assicurare la nostra salvezza, eppure l'esperienza ci ha insegnato che il nostro cammino attraverso i pascoli travagliati della vita non ha prodotto nulla di più nobile del lamentoso belare dei discepoli.

Perché avete paura? Come mai non avete fede? Le domande sembrano quasi fuori luogo venendo dal nostro Salvatore, quasi come se egli non fosse tanto paziente e longanime come speravamo. Ma Cristo ha posto un'aspettativa definitiva sui suoi discepoli che non è oltre la loro capacità di raggiungerla. Li stava chiamando a rimproverare la tempesta da soli? Avrebbero dovuto svegliarlo prima? Si aspettava che remassero tranquilli nella sicura fiducia? La Scrittura qui ci fornisce poche risposte, ma sappiamo che c'è una lezione duratura qui riguardo alla paura e alla fede.

Le tempeste sono una parte comune della vita, e nessun grande dilemma è piacevole. Mentre Paolo navigava verso Roma, sperimentarono un tempo …in cui né il sole né le stelle apparvero per molti giorni, e si posò sopra di noi non poca tempesta, e ogni speranza che ci saremo salvati fu allora tolta –Acts 27:20. In mezzo a una situazione cupa e senza speranza c'è una campana che continua a suonare chiara e luminosa: c'è una pace che può essere afferrata anche nelle circostanze più terribili. Paolo aveva passato un precario …notte e giorno sono stato nel profondo –2 Corinthians 11:25, eppure non pretese che il vento e il mare si sottomettessero alla sua autorità. Piuttosto egli dichiara che in mezzo alla tempesta …questa notte mi si presentò vicino un angelo di Dio, di cui io sono e al quale servo, dicendo: Non temere, Paolo… –Acts 27:23-24. Questa è una scena simile al pericolo sopportato dai discepoli (nel nostro testo di oggi) eppure vediamo un esito diverso. Paolo fu confortato e lodato mentre i discepoli ricevettero un rimprovero.

Mentre venivano sbattuti nelle fauci di una possibile tomba acquatica, i discepoli gridarono: …Maestro, non ti importa che periamo? –Mark 4:38. Quanto è naturale per tutti noi scaricare la nostra frustrazione e la colpa su un altro. Pensare che qualche persona apatica stia eludendo la propria responsabilità è molto scoraggiante. Allo stesso modo …il maestro della nave gli si fece vicino [Giona], e gli disse: Che significa per te, dormiente? Alzati, invoca il tuo Dio; forse Dio avrà pensiero di noi, che non periamo –Jonah 1:6.

Si percepisce un taglio nel rimprovero del maestro di nave molto simile alla risposta dei discepoli al Gesù dormiente. A Cristo non piace permettere che il male ci visitI, ma sembra non esserci un'altra vera via di grazia mediante la quale la sua pace possa inondare le nostre anime. Se prima non c'è valle, come potremo apprezzare la cima del monte? Se non ci sono spine, come godremo della rosa? Se prima non c'è tempesta, come apprezzeremo la calma? Paolo soffrì la stessa disperazione essendo …spinti a misura e oltre le forze, sì che disperammo perfino della vita –2 Corinthians 1:8. Eppure portava dentro il petto un'ancora visionaria per la sua anima.

Perché egli comanda e suscita il vento tempestoso, che fa levare le sue onde. Esse salgono fino al cielo, scendono di nuovo agli abissi: l'anima loro si scioglie per il dolore. Vacillano e barcollano come un ubriaco e sono fuori di sé. Allora gridano al SIGNORE nella loro angoscia, ed egli li trae fuori dalle loro afflizioni. Egli rende la tempesta calma, così che le sue onde si fermano. Allora si rallegrano perché si quietano; così li conduce al loro porto desiderato –Psalm 107:25-30.

The Desired Haven…

In qualche modo abbiamo abbracciato l'idea che il porto desiderato del riposo sia un'utopia euforica terrena priva di qualsiasi tempesta. Il maestro di bordo incaricato di guidare il vascello in rotta per Roma pensava che …il porto non era adatto per passare l'inverno… supponendo di aver raggiunto il loro scopo… –Acts 27:12-13, così salpò al primo accenno di approvazione dal vento meridionale. Ma il porto che Cristo promuove è un approdo libero da timori turbati e fede incerta. Questa è una pace … non come il mondo dà, io vi do. Non sia turbato il vostro cuore, né si spaventi –John 14:27. Questo riposo è nostro semplicemente navigando con Cristo e confidando che ci guidi attraverso ogni tempesta.

Le tempeste tenaci dell'avversità possono sorgere senza avvertimento tanto rapidamente come …un vento tempestoso, detto Euroclìdono –Acts 27:14. Questi venti tempestosi portano un'audacia sorprendente nel scuotere qualsiasi rapporto. Sentirsi tesi e all'erta in mezzo a situazioni stressanti è semplicemente natura umana. La nostra ghiandola midollare centrale scatena un potente ormone chiamato adrenalina nel nostro sistema, i muscoli si tendono, la mente si concentra, così siamo pronti a combattere o fuggire. Questo non è necessariamente ansia ma una risposta naturale. Come esseri umani, abbiamo la capacità data da Dio di ragionare in mezzo a passioni e pressioni estreme. I discepoli non sapevano cosa avrebbe fatto Gesù. Sapevano solo che la situazione era fuori controllo. Qui commisero il loro errore principale. Cristo sapeva Chi era al comando. Paolo sapeva Chi era al comando. Perfino Giona sapeva perché la tempesta era sorta. La nostra fede è destinata a fallire quando l'ansia aumenta e pensiamo di dover controllare le prove furiose intorno a noi. Possiamo avere un nobile programma e un cuore sincero e tuttavia ritrovarci con la nostra fede vacillante sfilacciata. Ci meravigliamo erroneamente che Dio sieda nei cieli e non faccia nulla. Lanciamo fedelmente le nostre preghiere verso l'alto, ma i cieli sembrano audacemente muti. Ci aspetteremmo ciò dai adoratori di Baal, di Buddha e dai apostati. Ma non dovrebbe accadere a persone con convinzioni forti—persone che sono nate di nuovo, frequentano regolarmente la chiesa, leggono la Bibbia e pregano quotidianamente. Dobbiamo riconsiderare che Dio non è tanto preoccupato per la nostra pace ambientale, quanto per il fatto che la nostra anima interna arrivi sana e salva al suo porto di riposo.

Quando siamo felici, rivendichiamo gioiosamente quel riposo, anche se non abbiamo la sensazione di averne davvero bisogno. Le sue inserzioni nelle nostre vite spesso sembrano interruzioni. Ma quando i tempi diventano disperati e abbiamo esaurito tutte le nostre risorse, ci aggrappiamo a lui con forza. In quell'ora straziante, spesso mette alla prova la nostra sincerità e non ci offre nulla … niente se non il silenzio. Cristo, che dorme nella nostra barca. Dorme… proprio quando abbiamo più bisogno di lui. E quindi la domanda, Perché avete paura? Come mai non avete fede? Francamente, questo mi sembra duro—perfino severo—e del tutto fuori dal carattere che mi aspetterei normalmente da Gesù. Ma la domanda deve essere affrontata, perché è necessaria se desideriamo entrare nel suo porto di riposo. I venti gli obbediscono, ma non ci obbediscono… o forse sì? Ovviamente non possiamo controllare il tempo, l'ambiente, le nostre situazioni o le persone intorno a noi. Tuttavia questi elementi esterni non sono la causa principale della nostra ansia. Sono le nostre proprie premonizioni difettose che martellano la nostra anima e ci impediscono di entrare nel portale della pace. I venti che sferzano il nostro vascello in una frenesia di paura non sono guidati da fuori ma scatenati da dentro. Questa ansia cavalca le onde dell'incredulità, mentre Cristo continua nel suo divino sonno, aspettando finché non riconosciamo la fonte della nostra ansia e gridiamo con fede. Questi quattro venti forti si risvegliano al minimo provocazione quando noi siamo…

…Preserving our Person

Se siamo sani, e se le cose vanno bene in famiglia e nelle finanze, potremmo essere inclini a interpretare male le nostre circostanze. È un errore credere che una navigazione facile sia un segno del favore di Dio, e che il problema sia un segno del suo dispiacere. Ogni dono buono e perfetto viene da Dio, ma anche una tempesta debilitante può rientrare in quella categoria. Il nostro contesto personale è temporale mentre la nostra anima è eterna. Dio frequentemente consumerà i nostri conforti personali per espandere la nostra fede. Ma nasce grande paura quando la nostra persona viene declassata. Molte delle nostre fobie sorgono in assenza di pericolo reale.

  1. La persona acrofobica ha paura delle altezze e teme di cadere da qualsiasi piattaforma anche se è sicura e ben protetta. Anche se innumerevoli altri vi si sono fermati con successo, egli è miseramente intrappolato in questa paura, non perché sia in pericolo, ma perché ha sopravvalutato enormemente la probabilità di cadere e rifiuta di credere alla verità.
  2. Lo zoofobico vive nella paura degli animali, creando immagini nella sua mente di essere dilaniato o sventrato.
  3. Il claustrofobico ha paura dei luoghi piccoli e stretti, mentre l'agorafobico teme i luoghi aperti.
  4. Arachibutyrophobia è la paura che il burro di arachidi si attacchi al palato della bocca.

Di fronte alla sua paura, il fobico può sperimentare il battito cardiaco accelerato, respirazione affannosa, secchezza della bocca, sudorazione, vertigini o capogiri. Così le loro fobie diventano reali per loro. Mentre la maggior parte scuserà il proprio difetto personale, la verità rimane che questa ansia è infondata. Quando scusiamo e favoriamo la preservazione della nostra persona, la paura è inevitabile. I discepoli temevano di perire, e Cristo chiese loro perché. Non è forse meglio …partire e essere con Cristo, il che è molto meglio –Philippians 1:23. Se possiamo fidarci di Cristo per la nostra vita, non possiamo forse affidarci a lui anche per la nostra morte?

Perché chi vorrà salvare la propria vita la perderà; ma chi perderà la propria vita per amor mio e del vangelo la salverà –Mark 8:35.

…Protecting our Property

All'esterno, la vita di Cristo fu una delle più travagliate mai vissute. I volpi hanno le loro tane e gli uccelli i loro nidi, mentre egli posava il suo cuscino nella parte posteriore di una barca che oscillava gemendo sotto la tempesta e il tumulto delle incessanti onde che vi si infrangevano. Ma il suo porto interiore era un mare di vetro. Questo era in parte dovuto al fatto che non aveva proprietà da proteggere. Anche la barca era presa in prestito. “Molto denaro, molta cura” recita il proverbio antico, e l'ansia sale quando la ricchezza diminuisce. E uno della folla gli disse: Maestro, di' a mio fratello che divida con me l'eredità –Luke 12:13. Gesù rifiutò di schierarsi con lui. Invece parlò al cuore avido che stava causando l'ansia. Se Cristo ci dà ricchezza, non dobbiamo sentirci in colpa. Se la toglie, non dobbiamo sentirci ansiosi. In mezzo alla tempesta ci è esortato …ad essere di buon cuore: perché non sarà perduta la vita di alcuno di voi, ma solo la nave –Acts 27:22. Questo fu somministrato come balsamo curativo ai marinai stravolti, ma per coloro che tendono a proteggere la propria proprietà è una saga sordida. Quando al giovane ricco fu offerta la salvezza in cambio della sua collezione terrena di gioielli, …se ne andò triste: perché aveva molti beni –Matthew 19:22. Coloro di noi che diventano ansiosi alla perdita della ricchezza non sono meno stolti.

…Perfecting our Plan

Partiamo per una rotta. Forse cambiamo lavoro, entriamo in una relazione o intraprendiamo qualche nuova via di ministero. Ci siamo lanciati nella fede e prima che ce ne accorgiamo, stiamo lottando. I venti e le onde della vita ordinaria sembrano lavorare contro di noi. Abbiamo aspettative che non vengono soddisfatte e sembra che Cristo non stia facendo la sua parte. Non è Cristo, ma piuttosto la nostra aspettativa che è la causa della nostra ansia. Ci aspettiamo molto dai nostri investimenti ed è scoraggiante vedere i nostri sforzi andare in fumo. Il polso di Marta si accelerò per la mancanza di aiuto che riceveva in cucina. La sua frustrazione aumentava mentre il pasto ben pianificato rimaneva incompiuto. Il suo lamento non è meno accusatorio di quello dei discepoli mentre remavano in mare. …Signore, non ti importa che mia sorella mi abbia lasciata a servire sola? Dille dunque che mi aiuti –Luke 10:40. La sua ansia non fu causata dalla negligenza di Maria né dall'indifferenza di Cristo. Sua sorella era ormeggiata al porto del riposo mentre Marta combatteva le tumultuose emozioni nel suo cuore. Così il perfezionista crea la propria tempesta quando la sua visione non realizzata non raggiunge le sue aspettative. Ma Cristo è più preoccupato dei petti pieni di fede che delle barche piene d'acqua.

…Pleasing all People

Le Scritture ci hanno insegnato bene ad amare il prossimo come noi stessi, ma questo non implica che dobbiamo sforzarci e mirare alla loro approvazione. È meraviglioso essere amati. È doloroso essere rifiutati. Perciò molte anime passano le ore di veglia cercando l'approvazione degli altri. Devono vestirsi come, comportarsi come, parlare come e vivere come i loro pari. Costoro vivono una vita carica di onde stressanti di ansia. Un turbine di “e se” arriva con ogni nuova conoscenza. Non esiste nave più fragile di una relazione. Non importa quanto grande sia il sacrificio che facciamo per essere amati, alla fine incontreremo una burrasca deludente che ci risucchierà negli abissi della disperazione. Quando i nostri migliori sforzi ci tradiscono e i nostri migliori amici ci deludono, dobbiamo portare il nostro vascello malconcio al porto del riposo. Relazioni scomode, sfortunate, spiacevoli e fastidiose esisteranno sempre. Faremo molto meglio a trovare scuse per il cattivo comportamento altrui che per il nostro. Quando sapremo rimproverare i venti che sorgono nella nostra stessa mente, ci ritroveremo immediatamente al porto desiderato.

Rimane dunque un riposo per il popolo di Dio. Perché chi è entrato nel suo riposo ha anche cessato dalle proprie opere, come Dio dalle sue. Cerchiamo dunque di entrare in quel riposo… –Hebrews 4:9-11.

And there arose a great storm of wind, and the waves beat into the ship, so that it was now full. And he was in the hinder part of the ship, asleep on a pillow: and they awake him, and say unto him, Master, carest thou not that we perish? And he arose, and rebuked the wind, and said unto the sea, Peace, be still. And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm. And he said unto them, Why are ye so fearful? how is it that ye have no faith? And they feared exceedingly, and said one to another, What manner of man is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him? Mark 4:37-41

Many times, I have read this passage and wondered what we are to derive from it. It seems to be a story that generates more questions than it solves. We often like to think of Jesus as the relational form of the Godhead; a sort of go-between, between us and the Almighty God. But here, in our scriptural passage, His behavior is almost unthinkable in human terms. How could Christ sleep in such a storm, much less in a boat filling with water? We can believe that He is Master of the wind and seas, and they must bow at His command, but does He expect us to do the same? Would our compassionate Christ expect us to be calm and fearless in such dire straits? Is all exhibition of fear the fruit of our lack of faith? These probing questions are disturbing, for we all would hope that our faith in Him is strong enough to secure our salvation, yet experience has taught us that our own walk through the troublesome pastures of life has produced nothing more noble than the harrowing bleating of the disciples.

Why are ye so fearful? How is it that ye have no faith? The questions seem almost out of place coming from our Saviour, almost as though He is not as patient and longsuffering as we had hoped. But Christ has placed a definitive expectation upon His disciples that is not beyond their attainment. Was He calling on them to rebuke the storm themselves? Should they have awakened Him sooner? Did he expect them to quietly row on in confident assurance? The Scripture here supplies us with few answers, but we do know that there is an abiding lesson here concerning fear and faith.

Storms are a common part of life, and no major dilemma is pleasant. While Paul sailed toward Rome, they experienced a time …when neither sun nor stars in many days appeared, and no small tempest lay on us, all hope that we should be saved was then taken away –Acts 27:20. In the midst of a cloudy and hopeless situation there is one bell that continues to toll clear and bright: There is a peace that can be apprehended even in the most dreadful circumstances. Paul had spent a precarious …night and a day I have been in the deep –2 Corinthians 11:25, yet he did not demand the wind and sea to submit to his authority. Rather, he states that in the midst of the storm …there stood by me this night the angel of God, whose I am, and whom I serve, Saying, Fear not, Paul… –Acts 27:23-24. This is a scene similar to the peril being endured by the disciples (in our text for today) yet we see a different outcome. Paul was comforted and commended while the disciples received rebuke.

While bobbing about in the clutches of a potential watery grave, the disciples cried out: …Master, carest thou not that we perish? –Mark 4:38. How natural it is for us all to thrust our frustration and blame upon another. To think that some apathetic person is shirking their responsibility is very disheartening. In like fashion …the shipmaster came to him [Jonah], and said unto him, What meanest thou, O sleeper? arise, call upon thy God, if so be that God will think upon us, that we perish not –Jonah 1:6.

There seems to be an edge to the shipmaster’s rebuke very similar to the disciple’s response to the sleeping Jesus. Christ finds no pleasure in allowing trouble to visit us, but there seems to be no other veritable vehicle of grace wherewith His peace can flood our souls. If there first be no valley, how shall we value the mountaintop? If there be no thorns, how shall we enjoy the rose? If there first be no storm, how shall we appreciate the calm? Paul suffered the same despair being …pressed out of measure, above strength, insomuch that we despaired even of life –2 Corinthians 1:8. Yet he carried within his breast a visionary anchor for his soul.

For he commandeth, and raiseth the stormy wind, which lifteth up the waves thereof. They mount up to the heaven, they go down again to the depths: their soul is melted because of trouble. They reel to and fro, and stagger like a drunken man, and are at their wits’ end. Then they cry unto the LORD in their trouble, and he bringeth them out of their distresses. He maketh the storm a calm, so that the waves thereof are still. Then are they glad because they be quiet; so he bringeth them unto their desired haven –Psalm 107:25-30.

The Desired Haven…

Somehow, we have embraced the thought that the desired haven of rest is an earthly euphoric utopia void of any storms. The shipmaster in charge of guiding the vessel en route to Rome thought that …the haven was not commodious to winter in … supposing that they had obtained their purpose… –Acts 27:12-13, so he set sail at the first hint of approval from the soft south wind. But the haven Christ promotes is a harbor that is free from fretful fear and fledgling faith. This is a peace … not as the world giveth, give I unto you. Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid –John 14:27. This rest is ours to be had just by sailing with Christ and trusting Him to guide us through each storm.

The tenacious storms of adversity can arise without warning as quickly as …a tempestuous wind, called Euroclydon –Acts 27:14. These tempestuous winds carry an amazing audacity to jolt any relationship. To feel tense and alert in the midst of stressful situations is but human nature. Our central medulla gland unleashes a powerful hormone called adrenaline into our system, our muscles become tense, our mind focuses, so that we are aroused and prepared for fight or flight. This is not necessarily anxiety but a natural response. As humans, we have a divine capacity to reason in the midst of extreme passion and pressure. The disciples did not know what Jesus would do. They only knew that this situation was out of control. Here is where they made their major mistake. Christ knew Who was in control. Paul knew Who was in control. Even Jonah knew why the tempest had arisen. Our faith is bound to fail when anxiety escalates, and we think we must control the raging trials about us. We may have a noble agenda and a sincere heart and still find our faltering faith frazzled. We mistakenly marvel that God sits in heaven and does nothing. We faithfully launch our prayers upward, but the heavens seem brazenly silent. We would expect that from worshippers of Baal, Buddha, and from backsliders. But it is not supposed to happen to people with strong convictions—people who are born again, attend church regularly, read their Bible, and pray on a daily basis. We must reconsider that God is not so concerned about our environmental peace, but rather that our inner soul arrives safe and sound at His haven of rest.

When we are happy, we jubilantly claim that rest, even though we have no sense of truly needing Him. His insertions into our lives often seem like interruptions. But when times get desperate and we have exhausted all our resources, we lean hard upon Him. In that excruciating hour, He often tests our sincerity and offers us nothing … nothing but silence. Christ, sleeping in our boat. Sleeping… right when we need him the most. And then the question, Why are ye so fearful? How is it that ye have no faith? Frankly, this seems hard to me—even harsh—and entirely out of character with what I would normally expect from Jesus. But the question must be answered, for it is necessary if we wish to enter His haven of rest. The winds obey Him, but they don’t obey us … or do they? We obviously cannot control the weather, our environment, our situations, or the people around us. Yet these externals are not the root cause of our anxiety. It is our own faulty premonitions that pound our soul and prevent us from entering the portal of peace. The winds that whip our vessel into a fearful frenzy are not driven from without but unleashed from within. This anxiety rides on the waves of unbelief, while Christ continues in His divine slumber, waiting until we recognize the source of our anxiety and call out in faith. These four strong winds are roused at the slightest provocation when we are…

…Preserving our Person

If we are healthy, and if things are going well in our family and finances, we may be prone to misinterpret our circumstances. It is a mistake to believe that easy sailing is a mark of God’s favor, and that trouble is a sign of His displeasure. All good and perfect gifts come from God, but a debilitating storm can fall under that category as well. Our personal surroundings are temporal while our soul is eternal. God will frequently expend our personal comforts in order to expand our faith. But great fear arises when our person is demoted. Many of our phobias arise in the absence of actual danger.

  1. The acrophobic person has a fear of heights and is afraid he will fall from the heights of any platform though it is secure and guarded well. Even if countless others have successfully stood there, he is miserably trapped in this fear, not because he is in danger, but because he has grossly overestimated his likelihood of falling and refuses to believe the truth.
  2. The zoophobic lives in fear of animals, creating images in his mind of being clawed to death or disemboweled.
  3. The claustrophobic is afraid of small, tight places, while the agoraphobic fears open places.
  4. Arachibutyrophobia is the fear of getting peanut butter stuck to the roof of your mouth.

In the face of his fear, the phobic may experience a racing heart, heavy breathing, dry mouth, perspiration, dizziness, or light-headedness. Thus, their phobias become real to them. While most will excuse their personal glitch, the truth remains that this anxiety is unfounded. When we excuse and cater to the preservation of our person, fear is inevitable. The disciples feared that they were perishing, and Christ asked them why. Is it not better …to depart, and to be with Christ; which is far better –Philippians 1:23. If we can trust Christ with our life, can we not trust him with our death?

For whosoever will save his life shall lose it; but whosoever shall lose his life for my sake and the gospel’s, the same shall save it –Mark 8:35.

…Protecting our Property

Outwardly, the life of Christ was one of the most troubled lives that was ever lived. Foxes had their dens and the birds had their nests while He lay His pillow in the back of a rocking boat groaning under tempest and tumult of the incessant waves breaking over it. But His inner haven was a sea of glass. This was partially due to the fact that He had no property to protect. Even the boat was borrowed. “Much coin, much care” states the ancient proverb, and anxiety rises when wealth falls. And one of the company said unto him, Master, speak to my brother, that he divide the inheritance with me –Luke 12:13. Jesus refused to side with him. Instead, He spoke to the covetous heart that was causing the anxiety. If Christ gives us wealth, we do not need to feel guilty. If He takes it, we do not need to feel anxiety. In the midst of the storm, we are exhorted …to be of good cheer: for there shall be no loss of any man’s life among you, but of the ship –Acts 27:22. This was ministered as healing balm to the bedraggled sailors, but to those who feel inclined to protect their property it is a sordid saga. When the rich young ruler was offered salvation in exchange for his earthly collection of trinkets, …he went away sorrowful: for he had great possessions –Matthew 19:22. Those of us who become anxious at the loss of our wealth are no less foolish.

…Perfecting our Plan

We set out on a course. Maybe we change jobs, enter into a relationship, or embark upon some new avenue of ministry. We have launched out in faith and before we know it, we are struggling. The winds and waves of ordinary life seem to be working against us. We have expectations that are not being met and it seems that Christ is not doing His part. It is not Christ, but rather it is our expectation that is the cause of our anxiety. We expect much from our investments and it is discouraging to see our efforts go for naught. Martha’s pulse quickened at the lack of help she was receiving in the kitchen. Her frustration rose while her well-planned meal remained unfinished. Her complaint is no less accusing than the disciples’ while rowing in the sea. …Lord, dost thou not care that my sister hath left me to serve alone? bid her therefore that she help me –Luke 10:40. Her anxiety was not caused by Mary’s neglect nor Christ’s indifference. Her sister was docked at the haven of rest while Martha battled the tumultuous emotions within her heart. So does the perfectionist create his own storm when his unfulfilled vision falls short of his expectations. But Christ is more concerned about faith-filled bosoms than water-filled boats.

…Pleasing all People

The Scriptures have taught us well to love our neighbor as ourselves, but that does not insinuate that we must strive and aim for their approval. It feels wonderful to be liked. It is painful to be rejected. Thus, many souls spend their waking hours seeking the approval of others. They must dress like, act like, talk like, and live like their peers. These live a life laden with stressful waves of anxiety. A flurry of “what ifs” arrive with each new acquaintance. There is no ship more fragile than a relationship. No matter how great a sacrifice we make to be loved, we will eventually encounter a disappointing squall sucking us down to the depths of despair. When our best efforts fail us and our best friends derail us, we must bring our battered vessel to the haven of rest. Inconvenient, unfortunate, unpleasant, and annoying relationships will always exist. We shall do much better to make excuses for others’ poor behavior than for our own. When we can rebuke the winds that arise within our own minds, we will immediately find ourselves at the desired haven.

There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God. For he that is entered into his rest, he also hath ceased from his own works, as God did from his. Let us labour therefore to enter into that rest… –Hebrews 4:9-11.

En daar het ’n geweldige storm van wind opgestaan, en die golwe het in die skip geslaan, sodat dit nou vol geword het. En Hy was agter in die skip, op ’n kussing aan die slaap: en hulle wek Hom op, en sê vir Hom: Meester, sorg U nie dat ons vergaan nie? En Hy het opgestaan en die wind aangespreek, en gesê vir die see: Stil, wees stil. En die wind het opgehou, en daar het ’n groot stilte gekom. En Hy sê vir hulle: Waarom is julle so bevrees? Hoe kom dit dat julle geen geloof het nie? En hulle was uiters bevrees en sê onder mekaar: Wie is dan hierdie mens, dat selfs die wind en die see Hom gehoorsaam is? Markus 4:37-41

Baie kere het ek hierdie gedeelte gelees en gewonder wat ons daaruit moet ontleen. Dit lyk na ’n verhaal wat meer vrae oproep as wat dit oplos. Ons dink dikwels aan Jesus as die relationele gedaante van die Drie-eenheid; ’n soort tussenganger tussen ons en die Almagtige God. Maar hier, in ons Skrifgedeelte, is Sy gedrag byna ondenkbaar in menslike terme. Hoe kon Christus in so ’n storm slaap, en nog minder in ’n boot wat vol water raak? Ons kan glo dat Hy die Meester van die wind en die seë is, en dat hulle by Sy bevel moet buig, maar verwag Hy van ons om dieselfde te doen? Sou ons meegevoelende Christus van ons verwag om kalm en vreesloos te wees in sulke akute omstandighede? Is alle vertoning van vrees die vrug van ’n gebrek aan geloof? Hierdie peilende vrae is onrusbarend, want ons sal almal hoop dat ons geloof in Hom sterk genoeg is om ons verlossing te verseker, tog het ervaring ons geleer dat ons eie wandel deur die moeisame weivelde van die lewe niks meer edels voortgebring het nie as die angswekkende gejank van die dissipels.

Waarom is julle so bevrees? Hoe kom dit dat julle geen geloof het nie? Die vrae lyk byna uit die plek komend as dit van ons Verlosser af kom, byna alsof Hy nie so geduldig en lankmoedig is as wat ons gehoop het nie. Maar Christus het ’n besliste verwagting op Sy dissipels geplaas wat nie buite hulle bereik is nie. Roepe Hy hulle op om self die storm te bestraf? Hadden hulle Hom nie vroeër moes wakker maak nie? Het Hy verwag dat hulle stilweg in vertroude vertroue sou aanroei? Die Skrif gee ons hier min antwoorde, maar ons weet dat daar ’n blywende les oor vrees en geloof is.

Storms is ’n algemene deel van die lewe, en geen groot dilemma is aangenaam nie. Terwyl Paulus na Rome gesegeld het, het hulle ’n tyd ervaar …waar geen son of sterre vir baie dae verskyn het nie, en daar het geen geringe storm op ons gelê nie, al die hoop dat ons gered sou word is toenemend weggeneem –Handelinge 27:20. In die midden van ’n bewolkte en hopelose situasie is daar een klokkie wat steeds helder lui: Daar is ’n vrede wat selfs in die mees verskriklike omstandighede vasgevat kan word. Paulus het ’n riskante …nag en ’n dag lank in die diepte gegaan –2 Korintiërs 11:25 deurgebring, tog het hy nie van die wind en see vereis om aan sy gesag te onderwerp nie. Inteendeel, hy sê dat in die middel van die storm …het in die nag voor my gestaan die engel van God, wie se ek is en wie ek dien, en sê: Wees nie bevrees nie, Paulus… –Handelinge 27:23-24. Dit is ’n toneel soortgelyk aan die gevaar wat die dissipels verdra (in ons teks vir vandag) tog sien ons ’n ander uitkoms. Paulus is vertroos en bemoedig, terwyl die dissipels berispe is.

Terwyl hulle in die kloue van ’n potensiële watersgraf rondgeslinger is, het die dissipels uitgeroep: …Meester, sorg U nie dat ons vergaan nie? –Markus 4:38. Hoe natuurlik is dit nie vir ons almal om ons frustrasie en skuld op ’n ander te plaas nie. Om te dink dat ’n apatiese persoon sy of haar verantwoordelikheid ontduik, is baie ontmoedigend. Op soortgelyke wyse …het die skipkaptein na hom [Jona] gekom en vir hom gesê: Wat bedoel jy, slaapkop? staan op, roep tot jou God, dalk sal God aan ons dink sodat ons nie verder vergaan nie –Jona 1:6.

Daar blyk ’n skerper toon te wees in die skipkaptein se berisping wat baie soortgelyk is aan die dissipels se reaksie op die slapende Jesus. Christus geniet dit nie om ergernis oor ons te laat kom nie, maar daar blyk geen ander werklike voertuig van genade te wees waardeur Sy vrede ons siele kan oorstroom nie. As daar eers geen vallei is nie, hoe sal ons die bergtop waardeer? As daar geen dorings is nie, hoe sal ons die roos geniet? As daar eers geen storm is nie, hoe sal ons die kalmte waardeer? Paulus het dieselfde wanhoop ervaar deurdat hy …byna tot niks toe bedrieg en baie swaar benoud is, so dat ons selfs die lewe hopeloos geag het –2 Korintiërs 1:8. Tog het hy ’n visionêre anker vir sy siel in sy bors gedra.

Want Hy gelas en laat die stormwind opgaan, wat sy golwe ophef. Hulle gaan op na die hemel en gaan weer af na die dieptes: hulle smelt, omdat hulle kommer het. Hulle wankel en swaai en is soos ’n dronk man, en hulle verstand hou op. Dan roep hulle tot die HERE in hulle benoudheid, en Hy bring hulle uit hulle benoudhede uit. Hy maak die storm stil, sodat die golwe daarvan stil is. Dan is hulle bly omdat dit gekalmeer het; en Hy bring hulle na die gewensde hawe –Psalm 107:25-30.

Die Gewensde Hawe…

Op een of ander manier het ons die gedagte aangeneem dat die gewensde hawe van rus ’n aardse euforiese utopie is sonder enige storms. Die skipkaptein wat die vaartuig op pad na Rome beveel het, het gedink dat …die hawe nie ruim was om daar te oorwinter nie … omdat hulle veronderstel het hulle het hul doel bereik… –Handelinge 27:12-13, en toe het hy by die eerste teken van goedkeuring van die sagtesuidewind uitgevoer. Maar die hawe wat Christus bevorder is ’n hawe wat vry is van angstige vrees en wankelende geloof. Dit is ’n vrede … nie soos die wêreld gee nie gee Ek aan julle. Laat julle hart nie ontsteld word nie, en wees nie bevrees nie –Johannes 14:27. Hierdie rus is ons s’n net deur saam met Christus te vaar en Hom te vertrou om ons deur elke storm te lei.

Die taai storme van teëspoed kan sonder waarskuwing opstaan net so vinnig as …’n stormagtige wind, genoem Eurokliedon –Handelinge 27:14. Hierdie stormagtige winde dra ’n verbasende dapperheid om enige verhouding te skud. Om gespanne en waaksaam te voel in die middel van stresvolle toestande is bloot menslike natuur. Ons sentrale medulla-gladsel maak ’n kragtige hormoon genaamd adrenalien vry in ons sisteem, ons spiere word gespanne, ons gedagtes fokus, sodat ons geprikkel is en gereed vir veg of vlug. Dit is nie noodwendig angs nie, maar ’n natuurlike reaksie. As mense het ons ’n goddelike vermoë om te redeneer te midde van uiterste passie en druk. Die dissipels het nie geweet wat Jesus sou doen nie. Hulle het net geweet dat hierdie situasie buite beheer was. Hier het hulle hul groot fout gemaak. Christus het geweet Wie beheer het. Paulus het geweet Wie beheer het. Selfs Jona het geweet waarom die storm opgestaan het. Ons geloof is voorbestaan om te faal wanneer angs eskaleer en ons dink ons moet die woedende beproewings rondom ons beheer. Ons mag ’n edele agenda en ’n opregte hart hê en tog vind ons eie wankelende geloof verlore. Ons verwonder ons verkeerdelik dat God in die hemel sit en niks doen nie. Ons rig ons gebede getrou op, maar die hemele lyk brutaal stil. Ons sou dit van aanbidders van Baäl en Boeddha verwag, en van afvalliges. Maar dit behoort nie te gebeur vir mense met sterk oortuigings nie—mense wat wedergebore is, gereeld kerk bywoon, hul Bybel lees en daagliks bid. Ons moet dit heroorweeg dat God nie so baie oor ons omgewingsvrede bekommerd is nie, maar eerder dat ons innerlike siel veilig en gesond by Sy hawe van rus aankom.

Wanneer ons gelukkig is, eis ons jubelend daardie rus, al het ons geen gevoel dat ons Hom regtig nodig het nie. Sy insette in ons lewens lyk dikwels soos onderbrekings. Maar wanneer tye desperaat raak en ons al ons hulpbronne uitgeput het, leun ons hard op Hom. In daardie pynlike uur toets Hy dikwels ons opregtheid en bied niks aan ons … niks behalwe stilte. Christus, slapend in ons boot. Slaap… presies wanneer ons Hom die meeste nodig het. En dan die vraag, Waarom is julle so bevrees? Hoe kom dit dat julle geen geloof het nie? Eerlik gesê, dit voel hard vir my—selfs swaarder—en volkome buite karakter van wat ek normaalweg van Jesus sou verwag. Maar die vraag moet beantwoord word, want dit is noodsaaklik as ons Sy hawe van rus wil binnedring. Die winde gehoorsaam Hom, maar hulle gehoorsaam ons nie … of doen hulle? Ons kan duidelik nie die weer, ons omgewing, ons situasies of die mense om ons beheer nie. Tog is hierdie eksterne dinge nie die wortel van ons angs nie. Dit is ons eie gebrekkige voorspellings wat op ons siel slaan en ons verhinder om die poort van vrede binne te gaan. Die winde wat ons vaartuig in ’n vreeslike woede laat sweef, word nie van buite aangestoot nie maar ontketen van binne. Hierdie angs ry op die golwe van ongeloof, terwyl Christus in Sy goddelike sluimer voortgaan, wagend totdat ons die bron van ons angs herken en in geloof uitroep. Hierdie vier kragtige winde word op die minste vooropkoms opgewek wanneer ons…

…Ons Persoon Bewaar

As ons gesond is, en as dinge goed gaan in ons familie en finansies, kan ons geneig wees om ons omstandighede verkeerd te interpreteer. Dit is ’n fout om te glo dat maklike vaar ’n teken van God se guns is, en dat moeilikheid ’n teken van Sy ontevredenheid is. Alle goeie en volmaakte gawes kom van God, maar ’n verlamende storm kan ook onder daardie kate­gorie val. Ons persoonlike omgewings is tydelik terwyl ons siel ewig is. God sal gereeld ons persoonlike geriewe bestee om ons geloof uit te brei. Maar groot vrees ontstaan wanneer ons persoon gedegradeer word. Baie van ons fobies ontstaan in die afwesigheid van werklike gevaar.

  1. Die akrofobiese persoon is bang vir hoogtes en vrees dat hy van enige platform sal val al is dit veilig en goed beskerm. Selfs al het talle ander daar suksesvol gestaan, is hy ellendig vasgevang in hierdie vrees, nie omdat hy in gevaar is nie, maar omdat hy sy waarskynlikheid om te val grofweg oorskat en weier om die waarheid te glo.
  2. Die zoofobiese lewe in vrees vir diere en skep beelde in sy gedagtes van geklou of uitbeelding tot die dood toe.
  3. Die klaustrofobiese is bang vir klein, nou ruimtes, terwyl die agorafobiese bang is vir oop plekke.
  4. Arachibutyrofobie is die vrees om, dat pinda-boter aan die dak van jou mond vasplak.

In die aangesig van sy vrees mag die fobiese ’n vinnige hartklop, swaar asemhaling, droë mond, sweet, duiseligheid of ligte hoof ervaar. Dus word hul fobies vir hulle werklik. Terwyl die meeste hul persoonlike defek sal vergewe, bly die waarheid dat hierdie angs grondloos is. Wanneer ons die behoud van ons persoon verskon en koester, is vrees onvermydelik. Die dissipels het gevrees dat hulle sou vergaan, en Christus het hulle gevra waarom. Is dit nie beter …om te vertrek en by Christus te wees; wat baie beter is –Filippense 1:23. As ons Christus met ons lewe kan vertrou, kan ons Hom nie asof ook nie met ons dood vertrou nie?

Want al wat sy lewe wil bewaar, sal dit verloor; maar al wat sy lewe verloor ter wille van My en die evangelie, sal dit bewaar –Markus 8:35.

…Ons Eiendom Beskerm

Uitwendige lyk die lewe van Christus een van die mees benoude lewens wat ooit geleef is. Vossies het hul nes en die voëls het hul voëlneste terwyl Hy sy kussing in die agterkant van ’n swaaiende boot neerlê wat kreun onder die storm en tumult van die onafgebroke golwe wat oor dit breek. Maar Sy innerlike hawe was ’n glansende see. Dit was gedeeltelik omdat Hy geen eiendom gehad het om te beskerm nie. Selfs die boot was geleen. “Baie geld, baie sorg,” lui die antieke spreekwoord, en angs styg wanneer rykdom val. En een uit die skare het vir Hom gesê: Meester, bestraal my broer dat hy die erfdeel met my verdeel –Lukas 12:13. Jesus weier om aan sy kant te staan. In plaas daarvan spreek Hy tot die begerige hart wat die angs veroorsaak het. As Christus ons rykdom gee, hoef ons nie skuldig te voel nie. As Hy dit wegneem, hoef ons nie angstig te wees nie. Te midde van die storm word ons aangespoor …om moed te hê: want daar sal geen man se lewe onder julle verlore gaan nie, behalwe die skip –Handelinge 27:22. Dit is uitgereik as helende salf aan die verslete matrose, maar vir diegene wat geneig voel om hul eiendom te beskerm, is dit ’n bittere sage. Toe die ryk jong heerser verlossing aangebied is in ruil vir sy aardse versameling snuisterye, …het hy weggeloop, bedroef: want hy het groot besittings gehad –Matteus 19:22. Diegene van ons wat angstig raak oor die verlies van ons rykdom is nie minder dwaas nie.

…Ons Plan Volmaak Maak

Ons stel uit op ’n koers. Miskien verander ons werk, begin in ’n verhouding, of begin ’n nuwe bedieningspad. Ons het in geloof uitgevaar en voor ons dit weet, sukkel ons. Die winde en golwe van die gewone lewe lyk of hulle teen ons werk. Ons het verwagtinge wat nie vervul word nie en dit lyk asof Christus nie Sy deel doen nie. Dit is nie Christus nie, maar eerder ons verwagting wat die oorsaak van ons angs is. Ons verwag baie van ons belegging en dit is ontmoedigend om te sien dat ons pogings tevergeefs gaan. Martha se pols het vinnig gegaan oor die gebrek aan hulp wat sy in die kombuis ontvang het. Haar frustrasie het gestyg terwyl haar welbeplande maaltyd onvoltooid gebly het. Haar klaende stelling beskuldig nie minder as die dissipels wat in die see geroei het. …Heer, sorg U nie dat my suster my alleen laat dien nie? Beveel haar dan om my te help –Lukas 10:40. Haar angs is nie veroorsaak deur Maria se verwaarlosing of Christus se onverskilligheid nie. Haar suster het by die hawe van rus aangekom terwyl Martha met die tumultueuse emosies in haar hart gestry het. So skep die perfeksionis sy eie storm wanneer sy onvervulde visie minder was as sy verwagtinge. Maar Christus is meer bekommerd oor geloofvolle borskamers as watergevulde bote.

…Almal Tevrede Stel

Die Skrif het ons goed geleer om ons naaste lief te hê soos onsself, maar dit impliseer nie dat ons moet probeer om hul goedkeuring te verkry nie. Dit voel wonderlik om geliefd te wees. Dit is pynlik om verwerp te word. Dus spandeer baie siele hul wakker ure op soek na die goedkeuring van ander. Hulle moet soos hulle maats aantrek, praat, optree en leef. Hierdie mense leef ’n lewe getooi met stresvolle golwe van angs. ’n Storm van “wat as” kom met elke nuwe kennis gemaak. Daar is geen skip broosser as ’n verhouding nie. Ongeag hoe groot ’n offer ons maak om liefgehad te word, sal ons uiteindelik ’n teleurstellende storm ervaar wat ons na die dieptes van wanhoop sug. Wanneer ons beste pogings ons verlaat en ons beste vriende ons laat ontspoor, moet ons ons beskaafde vaartuig na die hawe van rus bring. Ongemaklike, ongelukkige, onaangename en irriterende verhoudings sal altyd bestaan. Ons sal baie beter doen om verskonings te maak vir die slegte gedrag van ander as vir ons eie. Wanneer ons die winde wat in ons eie gedagtes opkom kan bestraf, sal ons onmiddellik onsself in die gewensde hawe vind.

Daar bly dan ’n rus oor tot die volk van God. Want wie in sy rus ingegaan het, het ook opgehou van sy eie werke, soos God van syne. Laat ons ons dus moeite gee om in daardie rus in te gaan… –Hebreërs 4:9-11.

“Why don’t we have a cure for cancer yet?” My patient asked me.

I shrugged. “There are lots of different kinds of cancer,” I said. “For some, there are cures, while for others we are still learning how best to treat them.”

“I think,” my patient said with the confidence that he was supposedly sharing a top-secret theory. “I think there actually is a cure for cancer, but the drug companies just don’t want us to know about it.”

I shook my head. “I think we are doing the best we can,” I told him. “We’ve come a long way when it comes to treatment of cancer, but we still have a long way to go.”

Cancer is a scary illness. One Christian man told me that he wasn’t afraid of dying, but if he had a choice, he would choose almost any other way to go than to die of cancer.

More than that, it is something that seems mysterious. More people seem to be getting it, yet no one really knows why.

In this article, I would like to take some time to explore what cancer is, and to discuss cancer screening tests. In the second part (in the next issue) Lord willing, I will discuss some of the treatments available for cancers.

I will mention here that I am a family doctor. I have cared for many patients with cancer, but I am certainly not an oncologist, nor do I know everything about cancer. What I understand, I am willing to share.

What is Cancer?

As with many things, we can trace the beginnings of cancer back to the fall of man in the Garden of Eden. We know that God created humans perfectly. As originally created, not only did they not have cancer, but they also would not have gotten it either.

In order to understand what cancer is, we need to understand how normal tissue and cells behave.

Normal cells live for a period of time and then die. This process is called apoptosis. It makes certain that there is a constant turnover of cells. It also prevents one type of cell from getting “out of line” and beginning to grow in a place where it doesn’t belong.

Every time our cells divide, they copy their DNA into the daughter cells. Usually this happens without error, but occasionally there is an error in the copy process. We call these errors mutations.

Cancer cells are cells that have lost the normal brakes on their behavior. Because of mutations in their DNA, they no longer have a limited life span, nor do they observe the limits of where they belong within the body. Instead, they begin to encroach on surrounding tissues, pulling in additional blood supply and nutrients in the process.

Cancer cells can enlarge locally, or they can spread through the lymphatic system or circulatory system to distant parts of the body. When cancer cells end up in other locations than where they originated, we call it metastases.

The type of cancer is determined by the type of cell that is multiplying out of control. Doctors don’t generally talk about “skin cancer,” even though there are cancers that originate in skin cells. Instead, they classify these cancers into basal cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and melanoma—each one referring to a different kind of skin cell. Each one of these skin cancers acts differently. Basal cell carcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma get bigger in a local area and seldom spread elsewhere, while melanoma is very prone to spreading to other parts of the body.

Additionally, how a cancer responds to treatment is going to be based on the type of cell that it comes from, not simply the organ where it originates.

Causes of Mutations…

We do not know how common cancer was in the days before the flood. I would speculate that it was fairly rare.

We know that before the flood, men lived to be very old—often into their 900s. Mutations must have been rare. Their DNA was closer to the original genetic specimen of mankind (and thus, to perfection) than ours is in the 21st century (AD) Therefore, the chance of genes mutating and abnormal genes popping up was much less than it is now.

…Environmental Factors

Beyond that, something must have happened around the time of the flood that increased the rate of mutations. Perhaps there was an increase in radiation levels. Maybe there were genetic changes that gradually caused cancer to show up.

Cancer is not mentioned in the Bible, although it is possible that Hezekiah’s “boil” could have been some kind of cancerous growth. It is also possible that some of the diseases that affected the Philistines when the ark of the covenant was in their land were cancerous tumors.

People began dying at younger ages after the flood and by soon after the time of Abraham, they were seldom living much past their one hundredth year.

Today, we know that things which damage a cell’s copying mechanism and its DNA increase the risk of cancer. The most well-known of these is radiation.

After the atomic bombs were dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki, survivors were noted to have significant increases in certain kinds of cancer. Leukemia (cancer of the blood) was the most common type of cancer, followed by cancer of stomach, lung, liver, and breast.

Radiation isn’t something that most people deal with on a regular basis. However, if you work in an x-ray department or if you needed to have radiation to treat some type of cancer, it is possible that you have been exposed to much higher levels of radiation than the general public.

There are plenty of other things that are associated with increases in cancers. Exposure to ultraviolet light increases the risk of skin cancer and is a big reason why doctors recommend sunscreen and protective clothing while enjoying the sunshine to limit ultraviolet exposure.

Finally, there are plenty of chemicals that are present in different types of work that can increase the risk of cancer.

…Unhealthy Foods

Foods that are high in nitrites increase the risk of intestinal cancers. Nitrites are typically present in smoked and cured meats. So, to be healthy, people should limit their intake of these foods to none or at the very least, a very limited percentage of the overall diet.

…Certain Prior Diseases

Another thing to mention is that certain types of infections can increase the risk of cancer. Epstein Barr virus, which causes infectious mononucleosis, has been associated with certain kinds of lymphoma. Hepatitis B and C increase the risk of hepatocellular carcinoma (liver cancer). And Helicobacter pylori infections in the stomach are associated with stomach cancers.

It is important to remember that just because someone has had one of these viruses it will not necessarily cause them to get cancer from that infection. Rather, it simply increases the risk that the person infected will get cancer at some point in the future.

…Unhealthy Habits

One last thing to mention is that certain toxins dramatically increase the risk of cancer. An obvious one is tobacco use, which strongly increases the risk of lung cancer, throat cancer, and even bladder cancer. Alcohol is another risk factor. Alcohol increases the risk of mouth and throat cancers, gastrointestinal cancers, and liver cancer. There really isn’t a safe amount of exposure to either of these toxic agents, but certainly the higher the level of exposure, the worse it is.

Screening for Cancer

There are many tests available that claim to be able to screen for a variety of cancers. Most of them are at least a little effective at identifying cancers at an early stage. However, there are a few problems with some of them which indicate that a certain test is ineffective at truly helping with the screening process.

A good place to start is to simply think about what a perfect screening test would look like. This will help us to see where tests might be beneficial or not.

A perfect screening test is going to have a number of features. First, it will have no false positive or false negative results. In other words, everyone who tests positive with the test will have cancer and those who test negative will not have cancer. Next, the test will identify the cancer at a point early enough in its development that it is easy to treat. The test will be cheap and minimally invasive, and it will require minimal exposure to radiation.

Unfortunately, no test that we currently do for screening totally meets these criteria.

For one thing, many tests produce both false positive and negative tests. These are both problems. The issue with a false negative test is obvious—it leads to someone thinking they don’t have cancer when they really do. A false positive test on the other hand leads to higher anxiety levels along with the cost and dangers from whatever ongoing testing is necessary to let a patient know that they don’t really have cancer.

An example of a bad test, in this respect, is the CEA-125. CEA-125 is a chemical that is made by some types of cancer. Oncologists use this level to track a patient’s response to chemotherapy.

It would make sense that you could use this as a screening test for these cancers, but it simply doesn’t work. Many people have elevated CEA levels, even though they don’t have cancer and on the other side, plenty of GI (gastrointestinal) cancers don’t make this chemical at all. Testing lots of people with CEA-125 testing will lead to more scans and biopsies, but it is doubtful if it would have a significant impact on death rates from cancer.

Another issue has to do with a particular cancer itself. In order for a test to be helpful, the cancer needs to have a long progression through precancerous stages until finally it develops into full-blown cancer.

An example is colon cancer. Most people who develop colon cancer have precancerous polyps several years before they get the cancer. This is why colonoscopies can be effective at preventing the progression to colon cancer.

If a patient has a colonoscopy, the doctor can detect the presence of polyps. More than that, he can remove the polyps through the scope, hopefully stopping the progression to cancer.

One last, related point is that there needs to be some benefit to early detection of cancer. If a new test can detect cancer six months earlier than existing tests, people will live an average of six months longer with the cancer than before, even if nothing else changes.

The question is whether diagnosing the cancer earlier leads to more effective treatment. Can you take it out before it spreads to the lymph glands and thereby completely avoid the need for chemotherapy?

If treatment and response rates are the same regardless of the stage at which you diagnose a cancer, then screening doesn’t really make sense.

The United States Preventive Services Task Force is a volunteer panel of experts that have reviewed the literature on a variety of tests. Based on the studies that have been conducted regarding the available tests, they make recommendations about the various tests and how often to use them.

This panel tends to be more conservative in their recommendations than many cancer societies. For instance, they recommend every other year for the use of mammograms for women between the ages of 50 and 75, as compared to the yearly screening recommended by other groups.

With each recommendation they give a grade of how good the studies are which support that specific recommendation, along with links for those studies. Their recommendations are well researched. This is helpful for low-risk people trying to decide what testing to do. If someone has a high risk because of family history or exposures, their recommendations are less helpful.

Cancer Challenges

People often discuss cancer as though it was a single entity. As before mentioned, cancer is not just one thing. Skin cancer behaves differently from lymphoma, which in turn behaves differently from sarcomas. The chance that there will ever be a single treatment for all cancer—the “Cure for Cancer” which people talk about, is unlikely.

An even bigger challenge when dealing with cancer cells is that they are very similar to our normal cells. Basically, we are trying to poison the cancer just a little more than the rest of our normal tissues. There are a number of different treatments that are currently available. In Part 2, we will address some of the different options available today and some others that may become available in the future.

Final Thoughts

There are a few things that come to mind when contemplating the subject of cancer.

We do not need to live in fear or make choices out of fear. Fear thou not; for I am with thee: be not dismayed; for I am thy God: I will strengthen thee; yea, I will help thee; yea, I will uphold thee with the right hand of my righteousness –Isaiah 41:10.

I don’t think that we should fatalistically allow anything to happen that might, simply because it is “God’s will.” We need to make wise choices, then having done so, we should not live in a state of anxiety.

Therefore take no thought, saying, What shall we eat? or, What shall we drink? or, Wherewithal shall we be clothed? (For after all these things do the Gentiles seek:) for your heavenly Father knoweth that ye have need of all these things. But seek ye first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you. Take therefore no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself. Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof –Matthew 6:31-34.

Finally, if we can, through wise decisions, prevent a certain cancer from forming or spreading, that seems like a reasonable goal. None of us will live forever in this body, but if we can die of something other than cancer, that seems like a good goal too. May God give us wisdom to care for the body which He has given us.
