As a child, you might think you can’t make a difference in the lives of people around you, but that is not true! Your little acts of kindness will not soon be forgotten. Being a true friend to someone who is hurting can change that person’s life forever.

This is the true story of “Hadassah” (not her real name) a young girl who was very much looking forward to starting school. Once she started first grade, what a disappointment it was to find that the second-grade girls were ready for someone to be mean to, or so it seemed. Maybe it would have been better if Hadassah had stood up to them, but she didn’t. Instead, she chose to act as if it didn’t hurt and tried to ignore them. Some days were better than others, but sadly this went on for three or four years.

Sure, there were good times too, but many evenings she walked home from school, crying most of the way and wishing that she wouldn’t need to go back to school the next day!

One day, one of the girls lost her pen. She was sure that Hadassah had stolen it. This was very disturbing to a very conscientious Hadassah. At the next recess she was blamed for cheating on her flash cards. Many other made-up stories were also passed around among the girls.

However, there was one little girl in that second-grade group of girls whose name we’ll say was “Esther”. She was Hadassah’s best friend and supported her all through those difficult years.

Esther was a very gentle, sweet girl, which is mostly what Hadassah remembered her for. Esther had cystic fibrosis and in the 1970s they didn’t have as many treatment options available for that disease as they do now, so those patients usually died very young. As Esther’s sickness became worse, the days that she felt well enough to be in school were rare. Since Esther was well-liked, the days when she was in school were special to everyone. Perhaps Esther realized she would be in heaven before the other girls—we don’t know for sure. But she taught the girls a song, “How Far Is Heaven”, which Hadassah still likes to sing today!

Hadassah still remembers seeing the emergency squad go past her house when they took Esther to the hospital for the last time. It was a very sad group of schoolgirls when Esther died at the age of 13. Esther had touched the hearts of many people in her short life, including the nurses who had cared for her during her stay in the hospital. Hadassah still remembers seeing some of the nurses crying at Esther’s funeral. Do you think Hadassah will ever forget Esther? Never!

Besides being her best friend, another bright spot for Hadassah was that when Esther was in school the other girls weren’t as mean to her (Hadassah). It so happened that in about the fourth grade, Esther was in school more often. One day she went home and told her parents what she was witnessing in school—how the other girls were against Hadassah and were being so mean to her. Esther’s father brought this problem up in the next parent/teacher meeting. What a night and day change started the very next day! One of the girls even came to Hadassah and apologized. Finally, they could all be friends and today those girls are Hadassah’s “old school friends”.

It’s worth it to stand beside someone who is being treated unkindly. Your support may be what God uses to help your friend to go through their hard times in a good way! And share it with your parents, they can help find a way to change the problem.

عندما كنتَ طفلاً، قد تظن أنك لا تستطيع أن تُحدث فرقًا في حياة الناس من حولك، لكن هذا ليس صحيحًا! لن تُنسى أفعالك الصغيرة من اللطف بسرعة. أن تكون صديقًا حقيقيًا لشخص متألم يمكن أن يغيّر حياة ذلك الشخص إلى الأبد.

هذه القصة الحقيقية لـ “Hadassah” (ليس اسمها الحقيقي) فتاة صغيرة كانت متحمِّسة جدًا لبدء الدراسة في المدرسة. ولكن عندما بدأت الصف الأول، يا له من خيبة أمل حين اكتشفت أن فتيات الصف الثاني كنّ مستعدات لأن يكنّ قاسيات مع شخص ما، أو هكذا بدا الأمر. ربما كان سيكون أفضل لو أن Hadassah تصدّت لهنّ، لكنها لم تفعل. بدلًا من ذلك، اختارت أن تتصرف كما لو أن ذلك لا يؤلمها وحاولت تجاهلهن. كانت هناك أيام أفضل من غيرها، لكن للأسف استمر هذا لثلاث أو أربع سنوات.

بالطبع، كانت هناك أوقات جيدة أيضًا، لكن كثيرًا من الأمسيات كانت تعود فيها إلى البيت من المدرسة وهي تبكي معظم الطريق وتتمنى ألا تضطر للعودة إلى المدرسة في اليوم التالي!

في أحد الأيام، فقدت إحدى الفتيات قلمها. كانت متأكدة أن Hadassah سرقته. كان هذا أمراً مزعجًا جدًا لِـHadassah الضميرية جدًا. في فترة الاستراحة التالية اتُهمت بالغش في بطاقات الاستذكار الخاصة بها. رُوِّجت أيضًا العديد من القصص الملفقة الأخرى بين الفتيات.

ومع ذلك، كان هناك فتاة صغيرة واحدة في تلك المجموعة من فتيات الصف الثاني سنقول إن اسمها كان “Esther”. كانت صديقة Hadassah المقرّبة ودعمتها طوال تلك السنوات الصعبة.

كانت Esther فتاة رقيقة وحلوة للغاية، وهذا في الغالب ما تتذكره Hadassah عنها. كان لدى Esther تليف كيسي، وفي السبعينيات لم تكن الخيارات العلاجية لذلك المرض متاحة كما هي الآن، لذا عادةً ما كان يموت هؤلاء المرضى في سن مبكرة جدًا. ومع تفاقم مرض Esther، أصبحت الأيام التي تشعر فيها بأن حالتها تسمح لها بالتواجد في المدرسة نادرة. وبما أن Esther كانت محبوبة، كانت الأيام التي تكون فيها في المدرسة مميزة للجميع. ربما كانت Esther تدرك أنها ستكون في السماء قبل الفتيات الأخريات—لا نعلم على وجه اليقين. لكنها علّمت الفتيات أغنية بعنوان “How Far Is Heaven”، التي لا تزال Hadassah تحب أن تُغنيها حتى اليوم!

لا تزال Hadassah تتذكّر رؤية سيارة الإسعاف تمر بجانب منزلها عندما أخذوا Esther إلى المستشفى للمرة الأخيرة. لقد كانت مجموعة فتيات مدرسية حزينة للغاية عندما ماتت Esther عن عمرٍ يناهز ثلاثة عشر عامًا. لقد لمست Esther قلوب كثيرين في حياتها القصيرة، بما في ذلك الممرضات اللواتي اعتنين بها خلال إقامتها في المستشفى. لا تزال Hadassah تتذكّر رؤية بعض الممرضات وهن يبكين في جنازة Esther. هل تعتقد أن Hadassah ستنسى Esther يومًا ما؟ أبدًا!

إلى جانب كونها صديقتها المقرّبة، كانت نقطة ضوء أخرى لدى Hadassah أنه عندما كانت Esther في المدرسة لم تكن الفتيات الأخريات قاسيات معها كما كنّ مع Hadassah. وصادف أنه في حوالي الصف الرابع كانت Esther في المدرسة أكثر. في يوم ما عادت إلى البيت وأخبرت والديها بما كانت تشهده في المدرسة—كيف كانت الفتيات الأخريات ضد Hadassah ويعاملوها بقسوة شديدة. طرح والد Esther هذه المشكلة في اجتماع الأهل والمعلمين التالي. يا له من تغيير بدأ بين ليلةٍ وضحاها منذ اليوم التالي! حتى أن إحدى الفتيات جاءت إلى Hadassah واعتذرت. وأخيرًا، استطعن جميعًا أن يكنّ صديقات، واليوم تلك الفتيات هن "صديقات المدرسة القديمات" لـHadassah.

من المجدي أن تقف إلى جانب شخص يُعامَل بقسوة. قد تكون مساندتك هي ما يستخدمه الله لمساعدة صديقك على تجاوز أوقاته الصعبة بطريقة جيدة! وشارِك الأمر مع والديك، فهم يستطيعون المساعدة في إيجاد طريقة لتغيير المشكلة.

Humanity is defined by its search for truth. Some people search for this truth through personal power, as they attempt to hold sway over their fellow man. Some search for truth in pleasure, seeing self-gratification as the greatest achievement in life. Others seek enlightenment through their own thoughts and reasonings, ever learning, and never able to come to the knowledge of the truth –2 Timothy 3:7. Yet others believe a life of service will be a reward unto itself, so they try to make a name for themselves through the publicity of their acts of service and charity.

Time and time again, throughout history, the collective thought of man has turned to something greater than themselves. Religions rise, and religions fall, empires are founded and crumble, philosophies develop and fall apart.

Against this background of intellectual undulation, a movement which most of my readers will recognize, took root in a small, mountainous region of the globe. Zurich, Switzerland, in the year 1525 AD, was to be its given birthplace and birthdate, but its roots had been established a full 1500 years earlier, in Galilee, where One taught and lived the final answers to all of man’s questions.

The beginnings of this more recent movement are well documented. In short, it was founded by a small group of assorted students, clergy, and commoners who sought after truth in its purest form. The stories of Conrad Grebel, Felix Manz, and George Blaurock are well known to many of us. They endeavored to separate from the spiritual corruption that surrounded them, as they established the beginnings of what would become known as the Anabaptist movement.

These three soon faced the scrutiny of the civil and spiritual authorities of their time, enduring hardship and suffering for their faith. Two of them eventually gave their lives for the truth they so esteemed. Felix Manz was the first Anabaptist to be martyred. On January 5th, 1527, not two years after his courageous re-baptism, he was drowned in the River Limmat which flowed through Zurich. His last words were: “Into thy hands, O God, I commend my spirit.”

The Anabaptist movement lived beyond these three men.

It spread and grew throughout Moravia, the Netherlands, Switzerland, and the Palatinate region of Germany. Almost one hundred years later there was another prominent leader in the Zurich hills; this one was an elderly farmer. He was well-seasoned in leading his flock through the ebb and flow of the challenges facing the believers of that time. His name is Hans Landis.

The year was 1613, January 26 to be exact. Converging on the small castle, Wadenswil, on the shore of Lake Zurich, was an elderly Hans Landis, along with fourteen of his church members. Most notably among these was Galli Fuchs, a schoolteacher and recent convert, as well as Bachman, a smith and well-known troublemaker, who had also been recently converted. There to meet with them were nine church and state officials, including the mayor of Zurich, Rudolf Rhan; his chief of police, Conrad Grebel (apparently a namesake of the original re-baptizer of nearly a century prior); and numerous local ministers from Zurich’s Protestant church. The reason for this meeting was that Hans’ spiritual work had been blessed, and his small congregation was rapidly growing, causing ripples in the attendance of rural parishes belonging to the Protestant church. Dropping attendance presented several difficulties to this combined church and state government.

First, the Protestant Church drew vast funds from its parishioners. Thus, another church drawing away and converting its members was seen not only as a spiritual threat, but also a financial one. The cantons of the area were often engaged in religion-fueled hostilities, ranging from angry debates to full-blown military campaigns. Second, deviant spiritual doctrines that disagreed with the government’s official religions were often introduced in times of civil unrest, and the peasant uprisings of nearby cantons were still fresh in the minds of local nobility and clergy. Events such as the Muensterites and their violent interpretations of Scripture remained a clear warning of religious zeal gone awry. These uprisings had taken place as the Catholic church collapsed in the area, which presented opportunities for new and sometimes extreme beliefs to take root. Now, the activities of Hans and his church seemed to these officials a matter bordering on rebellion and treachery.

This meeting was not the first encounter Hans Landis and his flock had had with the local authorities. An earlier investigation had been conducted, nearly four years prior. This report gave their meeting places as the forests, barns, and even Hans Landis’ home. However, no list of members was included, as even the Protestant neighbors of the church refused to name any of the Anabaptists. Not only did the local populace refuse to cooperate in naming any of those in Hans’ congregation, but it was also rumored that the Taufer held a general fund, in charge of Deacon Jacob Isler, from which they provided for needs within their community. To the officials, this appeared to be nothing more than another trick to persuade the poor of the community to forsake their church and join Hans and his group.

Mayor Rhan opened the meeting, addressing those of his company as “Reverend, high and well-learned, pious, noble, intelligent, wise, (and) dear lords.” Next, he spoke to Hans and the brethren with him, giving them a cordial greeting of “Honorable, dear and good friends” before reminding them of their positions by referring to them as “subjects”. Following these none-too-subtle maneuverings, he questioned them, asking for an explanation on “the reasons [why] you separated from our church and … started a separate sect.” Following this question, he assured them that the council wished to be tolerant but that the separatists should “not misuse the patience and graciousness of the lords.”

Meeting this introduction, Hans asked permission for him and his brethren to rise and address their “Gracious Lords”. Given it, he rose, thanking the mayor for his kind words of greeting before questioning their interest in the Anabaptists’ beliefs, as he maintained they had oft heard them before. He adjoined this by stating that all their doctrine was “nothing else than what Christ taught and what the apostles wrote.” As before, the Anabaptists asked simply to be allowed to hold onto this, supporting their government in matters not relating to conscience. They would also continue to pray for the government and their leaders.

Mayor Rhan did not take kindly to this answer, taking it as being implied that he and the Protestant church did not obey the commands of Christ. Hans, upon hearing this rebuttal, asked leave to take his group outside of the room for a short while. Upon returning, Galli Fuchs was presented and gave a testimony to the lords, outlining his spiritual journey through both the Protestant and Catholic churches, observing that while both preached well across the pulpit, both also denied this teaching by their godless living. Upon studying the Anabaptist faith and application, Galli was converted.

The officials were skeptical, arguing that Galli’s points had “still shown no reason for your separation.” Upon this rejoinder, another convert was brought forward, this one was the blacksmith Bachman. Bachman was immediately recognized by Conrad Grebel (not the Anabaptist founder), the Zurich chief of police, as having been known as one of the local rowdies—“It’s true, you were godless [and] there is no one in the entire area with whom I had more trouble than you.”

Bachman’s testimony echoed many of Galli’s points, especially on the purity and separateness of the true church, ending with this quote from Sirach: “Whoever stirs in pitch will be smudged.”

The debates continued, with contention flaring around communion, the examples of church leaders, and knowledge of salvation. As the meeting ended, Galli Fuchs could not resist a final remark: “If you would give us the church at Hirzel, … you would see … who would have the larger crowd!” This brought a round of laughter from the room, and Hans seized a final opportunity to speak, pleading: “Oh, dear sirs, let us remain by what we believe.”

Following this plea, the mayor deliberated, finally deciding that the brothers were to be given leave to go without arrest, who, upon exiting, were heard to speak in agreement: “We would also give life, body, property, and blood.” They were soon to have the opportunity to live this commitment.

Fifteen months passed. Hans was locked up in the Wellenberg tower in Zurich, along with Galli Fuchs, Deacon Jacob Isler, Hans Meili, Stephen Zehnder, and Paul Degia (a native of Milan, Italy). There they were held for fourteen weeks, and repeatedly cajoled, interrogated, and threatened. An order was finally handed down that they should leave the canton of Zurich, but Hans refused, to which the council responded with a threat often considered worse than death. The council maintained that because of these men’s civil disobedience, not their beliefs, they were to be sentenced as galley slaves to row aboard the ships of France in the Mediterranean.

Jacob Isler pleaded with the lords, asking them how they could do such a thing, knowing that the Taufer (Anabaptists) could not bear to leave their families. Stephen Zhender added: “We would not fear to go over sea and water since they [are] also the creation of God.” Despite these entreaties, the council made good on its threats, sentencing all six to the galleys.

The sentencing sent shock rippling through the community. The life expectancy for a young, healthy galley slave was no more than three years, and those three years would be filled with starvation, exposure, beatings, and exhaustion. Even in the harsher Catholic cantons, this sentence was severe. In the more lenient Protestant community, it brought public outrage.

The prisoners were all given one last chance to leave the canton, whereupon three of them relented. But Galli Fuchs, Stephen Zehnder, and Hans Landis steadfastly refused to change their mind. They were subsequently led under guard westward to a French ambassador in Solothurn, a town in the canton of Bern. Bern reacted in much the same way as Zurich had, with a ransom being offered for the prisoners’ release. When that failed, a file was secretly slipped into their cell in Solothurn. The prisoners’ chains were swiftly cut through, and they escaped the city, fleeing back to their homes. Once there, the populace, still outraged by their treatment, refused to report them to the authorities.

News of the escape spread and grew, and Hans was soon at work, baptizing the new converts, and even overseeing several marriages. The Anabaptists prospered, helping the poor of the community through food and no-interest loans from their alms fund. This renewed activity angered and frightened the authorities, who finally decided that the efforts of its elderly leader would need to be neutralized.

Hans was promptly arrested upon this decision and once again locked up in the Wellenberg. Here the threats and admonishments from the authorities were scaled up. If he would not recant or at least leave the canton, they would need to kill him.

Threats such as these did not sway Hans. He, instead, admonished the rulers not to commit sin in their treatment of him, affirming his resolve that he had “given himself to God” and “was ready to await what God would let come upon him.”

This brave stand by Hans brought a similar realization to the authorities: they would need to make good on their threats. Regarding Hans as a rebel, they maintained that he “wanted to be his own lord and master regardless of the honorable authorities,” and that he displayed the “stubborn, seditious resistance of wicked people.” Despite these allegations in conjunction with their threats, the magistrates realized that an execution would be an unpopular undertaking. Hans was well respected by the local populace, and even had connections in Amsterdam, where his daughter lived, being married to a Dutch Mennonite.

Officer Grebel, the Protestant clergy, and various others spent much time in discussion with Hans in his prison cell, but to no avail. By Thursday, September 29, 1614, they realized that he was completely immovable in his faith, unwilling either to recant or to leave the canton. This report, presented to the lords, sent them into deep deliberation. Some argued for publicly cutting off Hans’ ear and exiling him, while others deemed life imprisonment a more appropriate sentence. The matter was put to a vote at noon, and a majority decision was quickly reached. Hans Landis would be publicly beheaded at once.

Hans, upon hearing the decision, thought it only another ploy to persuade him to recant. However, upon approaching the well-known public execution site in Zurich, his face turned ashen, and his hands flew to his head. However, he swiftly composed himself, smiling and admonishing the crowd not to weep, as he trusted in his good hope. Noticing his wife and children present, he asked them to leave so that his resolve would not be weakened.

The sentence was read; Hans stood silent. Not a word of criticism had been raised against his personal morals. Instead, the issue was his refusal to disband his church. He remained steadfast, and so the executioner, Paul Vollmar, led Hans to the execution site. Some observers claimed that Vollmar let go of Hans, seemingly giving him a way of escape. When Hans did not, Vollmar raised his hands to God, asking forgiveness for what the law required him to perform. Hans, smiling, forgave the man, while various church ministers admonished him to recant, but Hans answered that he had seen no repentance in them.

Vollmar, having reached the site of the execution, gave Hans an opportunity to speak unimpeded, and Hans spoke but briefly: “I do not know what more I should say than that I wish everyone would come to a knowledge of their sins and repent, that they might be saved; this I would wish for everyone.”

Then, within sight of the place where Feliz Manz had given his life nearly a century prior, he knelt and bowed his head. The sword flashed downward, then Paul Vollmar asked the ritual question: “Have I executed this man rightly?”

“Yes,” came the reply, “you have executed this poor man.”

The immediate impact of the elderly Hans’ sacrifice was a ripple of support and outrage throughout the non-Anabaptist community. Rhudlof Rhan and Conrad Grebel continued to pressure the remaining Anabaptists, committing Margaretha Landis, Hans’s widow, to solitary confinement in the city hospital after her refusal to comply with their demands. Hans’s children would likewise remain strong, refusing to recant, but several of his grandchildren began attending the city church shortly after their grandfather’s execution.

The local Anabaptist congregation remained strong as well. Its spiritual descendants would carry the word of Christ with them when, a century later, a great emigration landed them on the wild shores of the New World. Here, in the religious freedom of Pennsylvania, they would establish new communities where the faith that had cost Hans Landis his life was to flourish through future generations. Today, there are believers throughout America who are endeavoring to live out their faith according to their conscience, who are where they are as a result of the life lived by Hans some 400 years ago. Some are his descendants, and some are friends of his descendants. May we be inspired to walk as Jesus walked, just like Hans.

L'umanità si definisce attraverso la sua ricerca della verità. Alcuni cercano questa verità mediante il potere personale, cercando di dominare i loro simili. Altri la cercano nel piacere, considerando l'autogratificazione il più grande traguardo della vita. Altri ancora cercano l'illuminazione attraverso i propri pensieri e ragionamenti, sempre apprendendo e mai giungendo alla conoscenza della verità – 2 Timoteo 3:7. Altri credono che una vita di servizio sia una ricompensa in sé, e perciò cercano di farsi un nome attraverso la pubblicità delle loro opere di servizio e carità.

Più e più volte, nel corso della storia, il pensiero collettivo dell'uomo si è rivolto a qualcosa di più grande di sé. Le religioni sorgono e cadono, gli imperi si fondano e crollano, le filosofie si sviluppano e si sfaldano.

Su questo sfondo di oscillazioni intellettuali, è nato un movimento che la maggior parte dei miei lettori riconoscerà, radicato in una piccola regione montuosa del globo. Zurigo, Svizzera, nell'anno 1525 d.C., fu designata come luogo e data di nascita, ma le sue radici erano state stabilite ben 1500 anni prima, in Galilea, dove Colui che insegnò e visse le risposte definitive a tutte le domande dell'uomo.

Gli inizi di questo movimento più recente sono ben documentati. In breve, fu fondato da un piccolo gruppo di studenti, chierici e popolani assortiti che cercavano la verità nella sua forma più pura. Le storie di Conrad Grebel, Felix Manz e George Blaurock sono note a molti di noi. Essi si sforzarono di separarsi dalla corruzione spirituale che li circondava, mentre stabilivano gli inizi di ciò che sarebbe divenuto noto come il movimento anabattista.

Questi tre affrontarono presto lo scrutinio delle autorità civili e spirituali del loro tempo, sopportando difficoltà e sofferenze per la loro fede. Due di loro alla fine sacrificarono la loro vita per la verità che tanto stimavano. Felix Manz fu il primo anabattista a essere martirizzato. Il 5 gennaio 1527, non due anni dopo il suo coraggioso ri-battesimo, fu annegato nel fiume Limmat che scorre attraverso Zurigo. Le sue ultime parole furono: “Nelle tue mani, o Dio, rimetto il mio spirito.”

Il movimento anabattista sopravvisse a questi tre uomini.

Si diffuse e crebbe attraverso la Moravia, i Paesi Bassi, la Svizzera e la regione del Palatinato in Germania. Quasi un secolo dopo vi fu un altro leader prominente nelle colline di Zurigo; costui era un anziano contadino. Era ben temprato nel guidare il suo gregge attraverso gli alti e bassi delle sfide che affrontavano i credenti di quel tempo. Il suo nome era Hans Landis.

L'anno era il 1613, il 26 gennaio per la precisione. A convergere sul piccolo castello di Wadenswil, sulla riva del lago di Zurigo, c'erano l'anziano Hans Landis e quattordici membri della sua chiesa. Tra i più notevoli vi erano Galli Fuchs, un maestro di scuola e neo-convertito, e Bachman, un fabbro e noto agitato, anch'egli recentemente convertito. A incontrarli c'erano nove funzionari della chiesa e dello stato, incluso il sindaco di Zurigo, Rudolf Rhan; il suo capo della polizia, Conrad Grebel (apparentemente omonimo del primo ri-battezzatore di quasi un secolo prima); e numerosi ministri locali della chiesa protestante di Zurigo. Il motivo di quell'incontro era che l'opera spirituale di Hans era stata benedetta e la sua piccola congregazione stava rapidamente crescendo, causando ripercussioni sulla frequenza delle parrocchie rurali appartenenti alla chiesa protestante. Il calo di frequentazione presentava diverse difficoltà a questo governo combinato di chiesa e stato.

In primo luogo, la Chiesa protestante traeva ingenti fondi dai suoi parrocchiani. Perciò, un'altra chiesa che attirava e convertiva i suoi membri era vista non solo come una minaccia spirituale, ma anche finanziaria. I cantoni dell'area erano spesso impegnati in ostilità alimentate dalla religione, che andavano da accesi dibattiti a campagne militari vere e proprie. In secondo luogo, dottrine spirituali deviate che contrastavano con le religioni ufficiali del governo venivano spesso introdotte in tempi di disordini civili, e le rivolte contadine dei cantoni vicini erano ancora vive nella memoria della nobiltà e del clero locali. Eventi come i Münsteriti e le loro violente interpretazioni delle Scritture rimanevano un chiaro monito dello zelo religioso degenerato. Queste insurrezioni si erano verificate mentre la chiesa cattolica collassava nella zona, il che aveva creato opportunità per che nuove e talvolta estreme credenze attecchissero. Ora, le attività di Hans e della sua chiesa apparivano a questi funzionari come una questione al confine con la ribellione e il tradimento.

Questo incontro non fu il primo scontro che Hans Landis e il suo gregge ebbero con le autorità locali. Un'investigazione precedente era stata condotta quasi quattro anni prima. Quel rapporto indicava i loro luoghi di riunione come foreste, stalle e persino la casa di Hans Landis. Tuttavia, non fu inclusa alcuna lista dei membri, poiché persino i vicini protestanti della chiesa rifiutarono di denunciare alcuno degli anabattisti. Non solo la popolazione locale rifiutò di collaborare nel nominare i membri della congregazione di Hans, ma circolava anche la voce che i Taufer tenessero un fondo comune, sotto la responsabilità del diacono Jacob Isler, dal quale provvedevano ai bisogni della comunità. Agli occhi dei funzionari, questo pareva nient'altro che un altro stratagemma per persuadere i poveri della comunità ad abbandonare la loro chiesa e unirsi a Hans e al suo gruppo.

Il sindaco Rhan aprì la riunione, rivolgendosi ai presenti come “Reverendi, alti e ben istruiti, pii, nobili, intelligenti, saggi, (e) cari signori.” Poi si rivolse a Hans e ai fratelli con lui, dando loro un cordiale saluto di “Onorevoli, cari e buoni amici” prima di ricordare loro le loro posizioni definendoli “sudditi”. Dopo queste manovre non troppo sottili, li interrogò, chiedendo una spiegazione sui “motivi per cui vi siete separati dalla nostra chiesa e … avete iniziato una setta separata.” Dopo questa domanda, li rassicurò che il consiglio desiderava essere tollerante ma che i separatisti non dovevano “abusare della pazienza e della gratuità dei signori.”

Di fronte a questa introduzione, Hans chiese il permesso per sé e per i suoi fratelli di alzarsi e rivolgersi ai loro “Signori Graziosi”. Concesso il permesso, si alzò, ringraziando il sindaco per le sue gentili parole di saluto prima di interrogarsi sul loro interesse per le credenze degli anabattisti, affermando che le avevano spesso udite prima. Aggiungeva che tutta la loro dottrina era “nient'altro che ciò che Cristo ha insegnato e ciò che gli apostoli hanno scritto.” Come prima, gli anabattisti chiesero semplicemente di poter mantenere questo, sostenendo il loro governo in questioni non relative alla coscienza. Avrebbero inoltre continuato a pregare per il governo e i loro capi.

Il sindaco Rhan non prese bene questa risposta, interpretandola come implicante che lui e la chiesa protestante non obbedissero ai comandamenti di Cristo. Hans, dopo aver ascoltato questa replica, chiese il permesso di portare il suo gruppo fuori dalla stanza per un breve istante. Al ritorno, fu presentato Galli Fuchs che rese una testimonianza ai signori, delineando il suo percorso spirituale attraverso la chiesa protestante e quella cattolica, osservando che mentre entrambe predicavano bene dal pulpito, entrambe negavano questo insegnamento con la loro vita senza Dio. Dopo aver studiato la fede e la pratica anabattista, Galli fu convertito.

I funzionari furono scettici, sostenendo che i punti di Galli “non avevano ancora mostrato motivo per la vostra separazione.” A questa obiezione fu portato avanti un altro convertito, il fabbro Bachman. Bachman fu immediatamente riconosciuto da Conrad Grebel (non il fondatore anabattista), il capo della polizia di Zurigo, come uno dei teppisti locali—“È vero, eri senza Dio [e] non c'è nessuno in tutta la zona con cui ho avuto più problemi di te.”

La testimonianza di Bachman ripeté molti dei punti di Galli, specialmente sulla purezza e separazione della vera chiesa, concludendo con questa citazione da Siracide: “Chi si mescola al bitume si macchia.”

I dibattiti continuarono, con contrasti che si accendevano attorno alla comunione, agli esempi dei capi della chiesa e alla conoscenza della salvezza. Quando la riunione terminò, Galli Fuchs non poté resistere a un'ultima osservazione: “Se ci dareste la chiesa di Hirzel, … vedreste … chi avrebbe la folla più numerosa!” Questo suscitò una risata nella sala, e Hans colse l'ultima opportunità per parlare, supplicando: “Oh, cari signori, lasciateci restare in ciò in cui crediamo.”

Dopo questa supplica, il sindaco deliberò, decidendo infine che i fratelli potevano andare senza arresto; uscendo furono sentiti dire in accordo: “Doneremmo anche la vita, il corpo, la proprietà e il sangue.” Ben presto avrebbero avuto l'opportunità di mettere in pratica questo impegno.

Passarono quindici mesi. Hans fu rinchiuso nella torre Wellenberg a Zurigo, insieme a Galli Fuchs, al diacono Jacob Isler, a Hans Meili, a Stephen Zehnder e a Paul Degia (originario di Milano, Italia). Lì rimasero per quattordici settimane, ripetutamente blanditi, interrogati e minacciati. Infine fu emesso un ordine che dovessero lasciare il cantone di Zurigo, ma Hans si rifiutò, al che il consiglio rispose con una minaccia spesso considerata peggiore della morte. Il consiglio stabilì che a causa della disobbedienza civile di questi uomini, non delle loro credenze, sarebbero stati condannati a remare come galeotti sulle navi di Francia nel Mediterraneo.

Jacob Isler implorò i signori, chiedendo loro come potessero fare una cosa del genere, sapendo che i Taufer (anabattisti) non avrebbero sopportato di lasciare le loro famiglie. Stephen Zhender aggiunse: “Non temeremmo di passare il mare e le acque poiché sono anch'essi creazione di Dio.” Nonostante questi appelli, il consiglio mise in atto le minacce, condannando tutti e sei ai galere.

La sentenza fece scalpore nella comunità. L'aspettativa di vita per un giovane galeotto sano non superava i tre anni, e quegli anni sarebbero stati pieni di fame, esposizione, percosse e spossatezza. Anche nei cantoni cattolici più severi, questa condanna era dura. Nella comunità protestante più indulgente suscitò indignazione pubblica.

Tutti i prigionieri ricevettero un'ultima possibilità di lasciare il cantone, e tre di loro cedettero. Ma Galli Fuchs, Stephen Zehnder e Hans Landis rifiutarono risolutamente di cambiare idea. Furono quindi condotti sotto guardia verso ovest fino a un ambasciatore di Francia a Soletta, una città nel cantone di Berna. Berna reagì in modo simile a Zurigo, offrendo un riscatto per la liberazione dei prigionieri. Quando ciò fallì, una lima fu furtivamente infilata nella loro cella a Soletta. Le catene dei prigionieri furono rapidamente tagliate e fuggirono dalla città, ritornando alle loro case. Una volta là, la popolazione, ancora irritata per il loro trattamento, si rifiutò di denunciarli alle autorità.

La notizia della fuga si diffuse e crebbe, e Hans si mise presto al lavoro, battezzando i nuovi convertiti e anche celebrando diversi matrimoni. Gli anabattisti prosperarono, aiutando i poveri della comunità con cibo e prestiti senza interesse dal loro fondo di elemosine. Questa rinnovata attività fece arrabbiare e spaventare le autorità, che decisero infine che gli sforzi del loro anziano leader dovevano essere neutralizzati.

Hans fu prontamente arrestato in seguito a questa decisione e nuovamente rinchiuso nel Wellenberg. Qui le minacce e gli ammonimenti delle autorità salirono di tono. Se non avesse abiurato o almeno lasciato il cantone, avrebbero dovuto ucciderlo.

Minacce simili non scossero Hans. Egli, invece, ammonì i governanti a non commettere peccato nel suo trattamento, affermando la sua risoluzione di essersi “donato a Dio” ed essere “pronto ad attendere ciò che Dio avrebbe permesso gli avvenisse.”

Questo coraggioso atteggiamento di Hans portò a una simile constatazione da parte delle autorità: avrebbero dovuto mantenere le loro minacce. Considerandolo un ribelle, sostennero che egli “voleva essere il proprio signore e padrone indipendentemente dalle onorevoli autorità,” e che mostrava la “ostinata, sediziosa resistenza di persone malvagie.” Nonostante queste accuse insieme alle loro minacce, i magistrati compresero che un'esecuzione sarebbe stata un'impresa impopolare. Hans era molto rispettato dalla popolazione locale e aveva persino collegamenti ad Amsterdam, dove viveva sua figlia sposata con un mennonita olandese.

L'ufficiale Grebel, il clero protestante e vari altri trascorsero molto tempo a discutere con Hans nella sua cella, senza successo. Giovedì 29 settembre 1614 si resero conto che egli era completamente irremovibile nella sua fede, non disposto né ad abiurare né a lasciare il cantone. Questo rapporto, presentato ai signori, li indusse a profonde deliberazioni. Alcuni propendevano per tagliare pubblicamente l'orecchio a Hans ed esiliarlo, mentre altri ritenevano più opportuna la pena dell'ergastolo. La questione fu posta a votazione a mezzogiorno, e una decisione di maggioranza fu rapidamente raggiunta. Hans Landis sarebbe stato pubblicamente decapitato immediatamente.

Hans, udendo la decisione, pensò che fosse un altro stratagemma per persuaderlo ad abiurare. Tuttavia, avvicinandosi al noto luogo di esecuzione pubblica a Zurigo, il suo viso divenne livido e le mani gli corsero alla testa. Si ricompose presto, sorridendo e ammonendo la folla a non piangere, poiché confidava nella sua buona speranza. Notando la presenza della moglie e dei figli, chiese loro di andarsene perché la sua determinazione non fosse indebolita.

La sentenza fu letta; Hans rimase in silenzio. Non fu sollevata alcuna critica contro i suoi costumi personali. Piuttosto, la questione era il suo rifiuto di sciogliere la sua chiesa. Egli rimase fermo, e così il boia, Paul Vollmar, condusse Hans al luogo dell'esecuzione. Alcuni osservatori affermarono che Vollmar lasciò andare Hans, apparentemente offrendogli una via di scampo. Quando Hans non colse l'opportunità, Vollmar levò le mani a Dio, chiedendo perdono per ciò che la legge gli imponeva di compiere. Hans, sorridendo, perdonò l'uomo, mentre vari ministri della chiesa lo esortavano ad abiurare; ma Hans rispose che non aveva visto alcun pentimento in loro.

Vollmar, giunto al luogo dell'esecuzione, dette a Hans l'opportunità di parlare indisturbato, e Hans parlò brevemente: “Non so cos'altro dovrei dire se non che desidero che tutti vengano a conoscenza dei loro peccati e si pentano, affinché possano essere salvati; questo lo desidererei per tutti.”

Poi, alla vista del luogo dove Felix Manz aveva dato la sua vita quasi un secolo prima, si inginocchiò e chinò il capo. La spada scintillò in basso, quindi Paul Vollmar pose la domanda rituale: “Ho eseguito correttamente quest'uomo?”

“Sì,” venne la risposta, “hai eseguito quest'uomo povero.”

L'impatto immediato del sacrificio dell'anziano Hans fu un'onda di sostegno e indignazione in tutta la comunità non anabattista. Rhudlof Rhan e Conrad Grebel continuarono a fare pressione sugli anabattisti rimasti, confinando Margaretha Landis, la vedova di Hans, in isolamento nell'ospedale cittadino dopo il suo rifiuto di conformarsi alle loro richieste. Anche i figli di Hans rimasero saldi, rifiutando di abiurare, ma diversi suoi nipoti cominciarono a frequentare poco dopo l'esecuzione la chiesa cittadina.

La congregazione anabattista locale rimase forte. I suoi discendenti spirituali avrebbero portato la parola di Cristo con sé quando, un secolo dopo, una grande emigrazione li avrebbe condotti sulle selvagge coste del Nuovo Mondo. Qui, nella libertà religiosa della Pennsylvania, avrebbero fondato nuove comunità dove la fede che era costata la vita a Hans Landis sarebbe fiorita attraverso le generazioni future. Oggi vi sono credenti in tutta l'America che si sforzano di vivere la loro fede secondo coscienza, che sono dove sono grazie alla vita vissuta da Hans circa 400 anni fa. Alcuni sono suoi discendenti, altri amici dei suoi discendenti. Possiamo essere ispirati a camminare come camminò Gesù, proprio come Hans.

This hymn is generally considered to be one of the greatest hymns ever written and is found in nearly every hymnal or book of hymns published today. It was written by a man who was frail in body, but strong in spirit. It was he who coined the phrase, “It is better to wear out than to rust out.” Let us now take a glimpse into the life of this servant of God.

Henry Francis Lyte, the author of this great and noteworthy hymn, was born June 1, 1793, in Ednam, near Kelso, Scotland. At a young age, he was left an orphan and was in comparative poverty. He was educated at Trinity College in Dublin, Ireland. It was there that his gift of poetry began to appear, winning him three prizes. His primary goal with his studies was to become a physician, instead, by the providence of God, he became a minister of the gospel of Jesus Christ.

One day in Cornwall, a fellow clergyman who was on his deathbed, requested that Lyte would come and give him some spiritual comfort. “To their mutual grief, they found themselves [both] groping for the light, veritable blind guides”. As they searched for truth and assurance of salvation, they fixed their faith on Christ, and Lyte came away from that sickroom a changed man, never to be the same again. It is said that it was his encounter with God at the bedside of that dying man that prompted Lyte’s noble hymn, “Jesus, I My Cross Have Taken.” In the year 1823, Henry F. Lyte took charge of a seashore parish, Lower Brixham, in Devonshire, England. It was at that place where he spent the last 23 years of his life toiling as a pastor for the spiritual good of the poor fishing people and the rough seafaring men of that region until his death in the fall of 1847. For all of Henry’s dedication and labor, he received a reward: having a Sunday school of several hundred scholars, as well as “a splendid company of seventy or eighty teachers, personally trained by him.”

Throughout his lifetime, his health was continually threatened by asthma and tuberculosis. Notwithstanding his physical frailties, he worked tirelessly with an established reputation as a poet, musician, and minister. Wherever he went, he was greatly loved and admired by his people. Toward the end of these later years, his health became gradually worse. So it was that during the winter months, he felt compelled to seek a warmer climate in Italy, which is a part of southern Europe.

Though he was greatly weakened by his sickness, on September 4, 1847, as Lyte was about to leave to head southward, he was arrested by an “irresistible desire” to preach once more to his congregation. He dearly loved these people and he had labored among them for so many years. “Against the protest of his amazed friends, he accomplished this purpose, and it is recorded that Lyte nearly had to crawl to the pulpit and his message came as from a dying man.” “O brethren,” he said, as he entered the familiar pulpit for the last time, “I stand here among you today, as alive from the dead, if I may hope to impress it upon you, and induce you to prepare for that solemn hour which must come to all, by a timely appreciation and dependance on the death of Christ.” These final words made a deep impact upon his congregation, after which he closed the service by administering the Lord’s Supper to his weeping people. Later that evening, after the service, he was inspired to “poetical composition” and wrote the eight stanzas of his last and greatest hymn:

Abide with me: fast falls the eventide;
The darkness deepens; Lord, with me abide:
when other helpers fail, and comforts flee,
Help of the helpless, O abide with me.

Swift to its close ebbs out life’s little day;
Earth’s joys grow dim, its glories pass away;
Change and decay in all around I see;
O Thou who changest not, abide with me.

Not a brief glance I beg, a passing word;
But, as Thou dwell’st with Thy disciples, Lord,
Familiar, condescending, patient, free,
Come, not to sojourn, but abide, with me.

Come not in terrors, as the King of kings;
But kind and good, with healing in Thy wings;
Tears for all woes, a heart for every plea;
Come, Friend of sinners, and thus ‘bide with me.

Thou on my head in early youth didst smile;
And, though rebellious and perverse meanwhile,
thou hast not left me, oft as I left thee:
On to the close, O Lord, abide with me.

I need Thy presence every passing hour;
What but Thy grace can foil the tempter’s power?
Who like Thyself my guide and stay can be?
Through cloud and sunshine, O abide with me.

I fear no foe, with Thee at hand to bless:
Ills have no weight, and tears no bitterness.
Where is death’s sting? Where, grave, thy victory?
I triumph still, if Thou abide with me.

Hold Thou Thy cross before my closing eyes;
Shine through the gloom, and point me to the skies;
Heaven’s morning breaks, and earth’s vain shadows flee:
In life, in death, O Lord, abide with me.

This hymn he gave to one of the family members that very night. Leaving the following day, he began his trek to Rome, Italy, hoping to gain some relief from his sickness. Lyte make it as far as Nice, France where his sickness prevented his further travel. He passed away soon after the age of 55, on November 20, 1847. His last words were “Joy! Peace!”

The scene behind this hymn is that of the resurrected Christ Jesus walking on the road to Emmaus with two of His somewhat sad and discouraged disciples. As they neared the end of their seven-mile walk and approached the village where they were going, Jesus …made as though he would have gone further. But they constrained him, saying, Abide with us: for it is toward evening, and the day is far spent. And he went in to tarry with them –Luke 24:28-29.

We can draw a parallel between that scene and Henry F. Lyte’s own experience of drawing toward the close of his earthly journey. Thus, as the disciples besought the risen Lord to abide with them in the close of that ancient day, so was the meaning of this song written in the “shadows of death” to the hymn writer.

Lyte himself composed a tune for this hymn on the same evening that he wrote it, but it never became widely used. However, the tune universally used was written fourteen years later by William Henry Monk, a noted London musician, and editor of the well-known Anglican hymnal, Hymns Ancient and Modern. He included this song in his first edition, which was published in 1861.

In all, William H. Monk composed 50 tunes for the hymnal. It is said that Monk, being “inspired by the beauty of a glorious sunset while yet experiencing a deep personal sorrow,” composed (in only 10 minutes) the tune, Eventide, for the song, “Abide With Me, Fast Falls The Eventide”. William Monk also wrote the music for other familiar hymns such as “Look, Ye Saints! The Sight Is Glorious”, and “The Strife Is O’er”.

To summarize, Henry Lyte experienced many sorrows during his lifetime. Both of his parents died at an early age leaving him an orphan. And his own sickness and frailty caused him to be in ongoing danger of asthma and tuberculosis. Yet, in spite of all his trials, we find in him a resilient spirit to reach out to others; to touch and minister the Gospel to those poor people among whom he lived. “In no other writer,” says Dr. Breed (in the Treasury of Hymn Stories), “are poetry and religion more exquisitely united.”

Ce cantique est généralement considéré comme l’un des plus grands jamais écrits et se trouve dans presque tous les recueil de cantiques publiés aujourd’hui. Il fut composé par un homme fragile de corps, mais fort d’esprit. C’est lui qui a forgé l’expression « Mieux vaut s’user que de rouiller. » Jetons maintenant un regard sur la vie de ce serviteur de Dieu.

Henry Francis Lyte, l’auteur de ce cantique grand et remarquable, naquit le 1er juin 1793 à Ednam, près de Kelso, en Écosse. Orphelin dès son jeune âge, il vécut dans une pauvreté relative. Il fit ses études au Trinity College de Dublin, en Irlande. C’est là que son don pour la poésie commença à se manifester, lui valant trois prix. Son objectif principal était de devenir médecin ; toutefois, par la providence de Dieu, il devint ministre de l’Évangile de Jésus-Christ.

Un jour, en Cornouailles, un collègue ecclésiastique sur son lit de mort demanda à Lyte de venir lui apporter quelque consolation spirituelle. « À leur peine commune, ils se trouvèrent [tous deux] tâtonnant pour la lumière, de véritables guides aveugles ». Alors qu’ils cherchaient la vérité et l’assurance du salut, ils fixèrent leur foi sur le Christ, et Lyte sortit de cette chambre de malade transformé, ne devant plus jamais être le même. On dit que sa rencontre avec Dieu au chevet de cet homme mourant a inspiré le noble cantique de Lyte, “Jesus, I My Cross Have Taken.” En 1823, Henry F. Lyte prit en charge une paroisse côtière, Lower Brixham, dans le Devonshire, en Angleterre. C’est là qu’il passa les 23 dernières années de sa vie, travaillant comme pasteur pour le bien spirituel des pauvres pêcheurs et des hommes de mer rudes de la région jusqu’à sa mort à l’automne 1847. Pour toute la dévotion et le labeur d’Henry, il reçut une récompense : une école du dimanche de plusieurs centaines d’élèves, ainsi que « une splendide compagnie de soixante-dix ou quatre-vingts enseignants, formés personnellement par lui. »

Tout au long de sa vie, sa santé fut continuellement menacée par l’asthme et la tuberculose. Malgré ses faiblesses physiques, il travailla sans relâche, ayant une réputation établie de poète, musicien et ministre. Partout où il alla, il fut grandement aimé et admiré par son peuple. Vers la fin de ces dernières années, sa santé s’aggravait progressivement. Ainsi, pendant les mois d’hiver, il se trouva contraint de chercher un climat plus chaud en Italie, qui fait partie de l’Europe du Sud.

Bien qu’énormément affaibli par sa maladie, le 4 septembre 1847, alors que Lyte s’apprêtait à partir vers le sud, il fut saisi d’un « désir irrésistible » de prêcher encore une fois à sa congrégation. Il aimait profondément ces gens et avait travaillé parmi eux pendant tant d’années. « Contre la protestation de ses amis stupéfaits, il accomplit ce dessein, et il est relaté que Lyte dut presque ramper jusqu’à la chaire et que son message vint comme d’un homme mourant. » « O frères, » dit-il, en entrant pour la dernière fois dans la chaire familière, « je me tiens ici parmi vous aujourd’hui, comme vivant parmi les morts, si je puis espérer vous l’imprimer et vous inciter à vous préparer pour cette heure solennelle qui doit venir pour tous, par une appréciation opportune et une dépendance envers la mort du Christ. » Ces dernières paroles eurent un profond impact sur sa congrégation, après quoi il termina le culte en administrant la Sainte-Cène à son peuple en larmes. Plus tard dans la soirée, après le culte, il fut inspiré pour une « composition poétique » et écrivit les huit strophes de son dernier et plus grand cantique :

Reste avec moi : tombe vite le soir ;
Les ténèbres s’approfondissent ; Seigneur, reste avec moi :
quand les autres secours manquent, et que les consolations fuient,
Aide des impuissants, ô reste avec moi.

Rapide vers sa fin s’écoule le petit jour de la vie ;
Les joies de la terre s’affaiblissent, ses gloires passent ;
Changement et déclin tout autour je vois ;
Ô Toi qui ne changes pas, reste avec moi.

Je ne demande pas un regard bref, une parole passagère ;
Mais, comme Tu demeurais avec Tes disciples, Seigneur,
Familier, condescendant, patient, libre,
Viens, non pour séjourner, mais demeure avec moi.

Ne viens pas dans les terreurs, comme le Roi des rois ;
Mais bon et aimable, avec la guérison sous Tes ailes ;
Des larmes pour tous les maux, un cœur pour chaque appel ;
Viens, Ami des pécheurs, et ainsi demeure avec moi.

Tu as souri sur ma tête dans ma jeunesse première ;
Et, bien que rebelle et pervers entre-temps,
Tu ne m’as pas abandonné, aussi souvent que je T’ai quitté :
Jusqu’à la fin, ô Seigneur, demeure avec moi.

J’ai besoin de Ta présence à chaque heure qui passe ;
Quoi d’autre que Ta grâce peut contrer la puissance du tentateur ?
Qui, comme Toi, peut être mon guide et mon appui ?
À travers nuages et soleil, ô demeure avec moi.

Je ne crains aucun ennemi, Toi à la main pour bénir :
Les maux n’ont aucun poids, et les larmes aucune amertume.
Où est la piqûre de la mort ? Où, tombeau, ta victoire ?
Je triomphe encore, si Tu demeures avec moi.

Tiens Ta croix devant mes yeux qui se ferment ;
Brille à travers l’obscurité, et montre-moi les cieux ;
L’aurore du ciel se lève, et les vains ombrages de la terre fuient :
Dans la vie, dans la mort, ô Seigneur, demeure avec moi.

Ce cantique, il le donna à un membre de la famille cette même nuit. Partant le lendemain, il commença son voyage vers Rome, en Italie, espérant obtenir quelque soulagement à sa maladie. Lyte n’alla que jusqu’à Nice, en France, où sa maladie l’empêcha de poursuivre son voyage. Il mourut peu après l’âge de 55 ans, le 20 novembre 1847. Ses dernières paroles furent « Joie ! Paix ! »

Le cadre derrière ce cantique est celui du Christ ressuscité marchant sur la route d’Emmaüs avec deux de Ses disciples quelque peu tristes et découragés. À l’approche de la fin de leur marche de sept milles et du village où ils se rendaient, Jésus …fit comme s’il allait encore plus loin. Mais ils l’obligèrent à rester, disant : Demeure avec nous, parce que le soir approche et le jour est déjà avancé. Et il entra pour s’attarder avec eux –Luc 24:28-29.

On peut établir un parallèle entre cette scène et l’expérience d’Henry F. Lyte qui s’approchait de la fin de son voyage terrestre. Ainsi, comme les disciples imploraient le Seigneur ressuscité de demeurer avec eux à la fin de ce jour ancien, telle fut la signification de ce chant écrit « à l’ombre de la mort » pour l’auteur du cantique.

Lyte composa lui-même une mélodie pour ce cantique la même soirée où il l’écrivit, mais elle ne devint jamais d’usage courant. Cependant, la mélodie universellement utilisée fut écrite quatorze ans plus tard par William Henry Monk, musicien londonien réputé et éditeur du célèbre recueil anglican Hymns Ancient and Modern. Il inclut ce chant dans sa première édition, publiée en 1861.

Au total, William H. Monk composa 50 mélodies pour le recueil. On dit que Monk, « inspiré par la beauté d’un glorieux coucher de soleil tout en éprouvant une profonde douleur personnelle », composa (en seulement 10 minutes) la mélodie Eventide pour le chant « Abide With Me, Fast Falls The Eventide ». William Monk écrivit également la musique d’autres cantiques familiers tels que « Look, Ye Saints! The Sight Is Glorious » et « The Strife Is O’er ».

Pour résumer, Henry Lyte connut de nombreuses peines au cours de sa vie. Ses deux parents moururent alors qu’il était jeune, le laissant orphelin. Sa propre maladie et fragilité le mirent continuellement en danger d’asthme et de tuberculose. Pourtant, malgré toutes ses épreuves, on trouve en lui un esprit résilient qui se tournait vers les autres ; pour toucher et servir l’Évangile aux pauvres gens parmi lesquels il vivait. « Chez aucun autre auteur, » dit le Dr. Breed (dans le Treasury of Hymn Stories), « la poésie et la religion ne sont plus exquisément unies. »
